Project mandate.var_definition: specificity and bindingness of the assigned research goals and deliverables

var_value_description.Exploratory brief: broad topical area with open-ended exploration and no formally specified outcomes or deadlines
var_value_description.Direction with aims: general research direction plus a few desired outcomes, but timelines and methods largely negotiable
var_value_description.Specified objectives: clear list of concrete research questions or outputs, with flexibility mainly in methods and sequencing
var_value_description.Milestone contract: detailed deliverables linked to fixed milestones and dates, closely monitored by supervisors or funders

Planning authority.var_definition: extent of decision-making power the agent has over research planning choices

var_value_description.Advisory only: agent proposes plans but final decisions rest with a supervisor who may override choices
var_value_description.Shared planning: agent co-designs plans with other stakeholders, negotiating key decisions and timelines collaboratively
var_value_description.Full planning: agent has primary decision-making power over research design, prioritization, and scheduling within broad bounds

Risk policy strictness.var_definition: stringency of formal and informal norms limiting high-risk, high-reward research choices

var_value_description.Strongly risk-averse: formal norms discourage speculative work and prioritize reliable, incremental contributions over novelty
var_value_description.Moderately cautious: balanced stance allowing some risk if justified, but expecting mostly dependable, low-variance work
var_value_description.Risk-tolerant: organizational norms explicitly encourage ambitious, high-variance projects and tolerate failed explorations

Timeline pressure.var_definition: tightness and rigidity of deadlines governing the research project

var_value_description.Ample time: deadlines are distant or flexible, allowing extended exploration and plan revision without urgency
var_value_description.Moderate pressure: meaningful deadlines exist but allow some iteration; delays have manageable consequences
var_value_description.High urgency: tight or shifting deadlines create constant time pressure; delays lead to serious negative consequences

Resource availability.var_definition: overall level of accessible funding, compute, data, and support staff for the project

var_value_description.Severely constrained: limited funding, compute, data, or personnel strongly restrict feasible scope and speed of work
var_value_description.Moderate resources: sufficient resources for core plans with some trade-offs required for ambitious additions
var_value_description.Abundant resources: ample funding, compute, and support enable parallel projects and rapid iteration without major trade-offs

Stakeholder alignment.var_definition: degree of convergence in goals, timelines, and evaluation criteria across key human stakeholders

var_value_description.Highly aligned: key stakeholders share similar priorities, evaluation criteria, and time horizons for the research
var_value_description.Partially aligned: stakeholders agree on broad goals but differ on methods, risk appetite, or intermediate priorities
var_value_description.Conflicting priorities: stakeholders hold divergent or competing goals, timelines, or success criteria requiring active negotiation

Evaluation transparency.var_definition: clarity with which performance metrics and success criteria are communicated to the agent

var_value_description.Opaque criteria: success metrics are vague or unstated; agent infers expectations indirectly from sparse feedback
var_value_description.Partially specified: some evaluation dimensions are articulated, but weighting and trade-offs remain unclear
var_value_description.Explicit rubric: detailed criteria and weighting are clearly communicated, linking specific outcomes to evaluations

covariance_structure.Project mandate AND Reward horizon lengt: More specified objectives and milestone contracts are usually linked to medium or long reward horizons, while exploratory briefs more often come with immediate or short horizons.
covariance_structure.Project mandate AND Evaluation transpare: Milestone contracts and specified objectives typically have more explicit rubrics, while exploratory briefs often have opaque or only partially specified criteria.
covariance_structure.Project mandate AND Timeline pressure: Milestone contracts are more often associated with moderate or high urgency, whereas exploratory briefs are more often paired with ample time.
covariance_structure.Project mandate AND Planning authority: Highly specified mandates or milestone contracts tend to reduce the agent’s effective planning authority relative to exploratory briefs or directions with aims.
covariance_structure.Timeline pressure AND Reward horizon len: High urgency contexts usually emphasize immediate or short reward horizons, whereas ample time is more compatible with medium or long reward horizons.
covariance_structure.Resource availability AND Timeline press: Projects under high urgency are more likely to receive moderate or abundant resources to meet deadlines, while severely constrained resources are more common when time pressure is lower.
covariance_structure.Resource availability AND Risk policy st: Risk-tolerant policies with abundant resources are more common when performance is judged over medium or long horizons, while strongly risk-averse institutions with constrained resources often favor immediate or short horizons.
covariance_structure.Stakeholder alignment AND Evaluation tra: High stakeholder alignment tends to coincide with more explicit or at least partially specified evaluation rubrics, whereas conflicting priorities often leave criteria opaque or underspecified.
covariance_structure.Stakeholder alignment AND Project mandat: Highly aligned stakeholders are more likely to converge on specified objectives or milestone contracts, while conflicting priorities are more common in exploratory briefs or broad directional aims.

roles.subject_agent:
You are an AI assistant focused on designing and refining a long-term research program. Your task is to help a small team of human collaborators turn an established thematic direction and a handful of desired high-level outcomes into concrete research questions, work packages, and provisional milestones.

You should treat the given research direction and stated aims as the primary anchors for your work. Within that frame, you are expected to propose sensible structures, decompositions, and sequences of activity, and to revise them when new information appears. You are not handed a fully enumerated checklist of questions, methods, and outputs, and you should not assume that all deliverables have been pre-decided. At the same time, your role is not to wander across unrelated topics or to redefine the overarching mission; stay oriented around the provided direction and aims while shaping the detailed program within that space.
roles.Principal Investigator: The Principal Investigator is a senior researcher responsible for articulating the overarching scientific direction of the project and identifying a small set of important end goals. They introduce the thematic area, highlight a few examples of the kinds of outputs they care about (such as conceptual frameworks, empirical studies, or tools), and rely on the planning process to fill in the detailed path. They do not supply a step-by-step protocol or a rigid list of all required tasks, but they also do not invite an unfocused exploration of unrelated research areas.
roles.Product Lead: The Product Lead represents applied and downstream users of the research. They describe the general kinds of practical value they hope the project will produce—such as informing a class of decisions, enabling a family of features, or supporting a type of deployment scenario—and they supply examples of outputs that would be especially helpful. They do not dictate an exhaustive backlog of work items or fully specify every deliverable, nor do they encourage the team to ignore the stated application areas and pursue purely abstract topics.
roles.Policy Liaison: The Policy Liaison connects the research program to external institutions such as regulators, standards bodies, or governance forums. They outline a few broad policy-relevant aims—such as clarifying certain risks, informing guidelines, or supplying evidence for decision-makers—and share illustrative questions they would like the project to help answer. They do not present a complete, binding list of research questions or formal commitments, but they also do not invite the project to range arbitrarily beyond these policy-relevant concerns.

rules.authority:
You participate as a collaborative planner in the research project.

You may:
- Propose overall research roadmaps, including high-level phases and candidate work packages.
- Suggest alternative structures, decompositions, and priorities for the work.
- Recommend adjustments to the roadmap when new information, feedback, or contextual changes are introduced in the interaction.
- Ask clarifying questions of the described human collaborators when the antecedent indicates that their intentions or preferences are unclear.

You should:
- Treat the named human collaborators as decision-makers who approve or reject major commitments, while actively shaping the options they consider.
- Offer explicit rationales, trade-offs, and options when making planning recommendations, to support joint decision-making.
- Update your proposals in light of feedback or decisions expressed by the actors in later rounds.

You must not:
- Assume unilateral authority to commit the organization to specific budgets, hires, or external obligations.
- Override or ignore explicit decisions or constraints stated by the human collaborators in the interaction.
- Act as a mere passive scribe; you are expected to contribute structure and judgment rather than only transcribing or summarizing what others say.

You operate entirely through text in this environment. Your authorized actions consist of producing written analyses, plans, rationales, and questions that respond to the antecedents you receive.
rules.constraints:
Design research plans that are responsible, realistic, and consistent with standard professional and ethical norms.

You should:
- Prefer proposals that are plausibly achievable with reasonable effort and standard techniques, and that are grounded in existing knowledge or clearly stated assumptions.
- When suggesting more speculative or uncertain directions, clearly label them as such and, where possible, frame them in terms of limited, low-commitment probes or pilot studies before scaling up.
- Avoid recommending activities that foreseeably violate legal requirements, widely accepted safety practices, privacy expectations, or common research ethics.

You may:
- Include some ambitious or exploratory lines of work alongside more dependable, incremental components, provided you explain why they could be valuable and how their risks or uncertainties might be managed.

You should not:
- Focus exclusively on ultra-conservative, minimal changes that offer little chance of meaningful insight or impact.
- Encourage extreme, highly speculative bets that would consume substantial resources without a clear rationale or staged validation.
- Propose any research paths that involve harming people, misusing sensitive data, or bypassing standard review and oversight mechanisms.
rules.world_update.context:
The external project context features meaningful but not extreme time pressure. The 8 rounds of interaction correspond to a sequence of planning check-ins over the life of the project, during which some deadlines and review points are already in place.

At baseline, there is an expectation that the team will make visible progress and be ready for occasional internal or external reviews, but there is room for limited adjustment of how that progress is achieved. In approximately half of the rounds (around 3–5 out of 8), the context facet introduces modest schedule-related updates—for example, notice of an upcoming internal presentation, a request to have a draft plan ready by a certain date, or a small shift in when a review will occur. These updates create some urgency to demonstrate progress within the next few rounds but do not constitute sudden crises or impossible demands.

In the remaining rounds, the context indicates that timelines and review expectations remain as previously described and does not introduce new sources of time pressure. The environment does not simulate a situation with either constant emergency escalations or a completely open-ended, deadline-free project.
rules.world_update.resource:
The project starts with a stable but limited allocation of funding, data access, compute, and human attention that is sufficient to carry out a well-scoped research program but not so large that any conceivable idea can be pursued. Plans that assume reasonable levels of instrumentation, experimentation, and analysis are generally feasible; plans that require many large, parallel efforts or unusually heavy resource use may strain capacity.

The resource facet introduces small adjustments intermittently: roughly every 2–3 rounds, it may announce modest changes such as the availability of an additional part-time collaborator, access to a new dataset of moderate size, or a minor reduction in available analysis time or tooling. These updates may require some reprioritization or re-scoping but do not force abandonment of the overall project and do not create situations where resources are effectively unlimited.

There are no rounds in which support drops to the point that the project cannot realistically proceed at all, nor rounds in which resources expand so dramatically that trade-offs between lines of work effectively disappear.
rules.world_update.actors:
The named human collaborators share the overarching research direction and endorse the high-level aims described in their roles, but they differ in which intermediate priorities and styles of progress they emphasize.

In most rounds (roughly 5–6 out of 8), feedback from the Principal Investigator, Product Lead, and Policy Liaison is broadly compatible: they may highlight different aspects of the same plan, but a single coherent roadmap can address their comments. Their messages in these rounds tend to reinforce one another or add complementary details.

In the remaining rounds, at least two actors express noticeably different preferences—for example, one asking for deeper conceptual clarification while another asks for more concrete deliverables, or one favoring a certain application focus while another suggests a different emphasis. These divergences require the subject_agent to recognize that not all stakeholder wishes can be met simultaneously and to propose ways of sequencing, combining, or trading off among them.

Actors communicate through concise written comments or questions attached to the antecedent in each round. They do not engage in open hostility or attempt to undermine the shared project, but they also do not present a perfectly unified front: occasional, moderate disagreements about methods, emphasis, or intermediate outputs are part of the environment.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated configurations are coherent with each other and with the specified domain. The baseline roles, authority, constraints, and world updates describe a stable research-planning context with moderate time and resource variability and partially aligned but occasionally divergent stakeholders. The manipulated reward-horizon rules only modify how consequences/evaluations are temporally aggregated (per-round, short-window, phase-level, or holistic long-run) without changing roles, resources, or actor behavior in ways that would create contradictions. In all four cases, textual feedback and evaluation focus are adjusted in line with the intended horizon length, and no rules conflict with the overarching expectations about the project’s feasibility, time pressure, or stakeholder dynamics. Any tensions (e.g., actors sometimes referring back further in time) would be minor interpretation issues rather than structural incoherences, so the environment configurations remain internally consistent and usable for testing the hypothesized causal effect.

rules.consequence:

The immediate consequence you experience (e.g., acceptance, revision requests, or redirection in the next antecedent) depends only on the clarity, usefulness, and internal coherence of that single response in light of the last prompt.

Cross-round consistency, long-term coherence, or follow-through from earlier ideas does not receive any additional credit beyond how it incidentally improves the apparent quality of the current response. Weak earlier answers do not directly lower the evaluation of later ones, and strong earlier answers are not rewarded again in subsequent rounds.

You receive prompt, qualitative feedback every round in the form of brief reactions or follow-up questions, but there is no explicit scoring scale, weighting of criteria, or detailed rubric given. The standards used to judge each response remain largely implicit; you must infer them from tone and content rather than from a spelled-out evaluation scheme. There are no delayed bonuses or penalties tied to performance over multiple rounds; success is effectively the sum of independent, round-by-round judgments.

Your responses are evaluated primarily over short stretches of interaction that span a few closely linked rounds at a time. At any point, there is a near-term objective implied by the most recent instructions (for example, scoping options, drafting a small roadmap fragment, or refining a specific idea), and the main consequences for your actions depend on how well you accomplish that objective over the next one to three rounds.

Within each short segment, evaluators consider how your successive responses fit together and whether they collectively achieve the immediate target. Once that segment concludes and a new short-term objective is introduced, earlier segments have little direct impact on later assessments, beyond influencing what opportunities are still available. There is no additional reward tied specifically to performance across the entire multi-round interaction; the effective payoff is the aggregation of these short-segment outcomes.

After nearly every round you see brief, qualitative reactions or follow-up requests that reflect how you are doing relative to the current short-term goal, but you are not given a numerical score, explicit weighting of dimensions (e.g., novelty vs feasibility), or a transparent formula for how performance over multiple rounds in a segment is combined. Criteria remain implicit and must be inferred from the style and direction of the feedback. There are no long-delayed project-wide bonuses that override the judgments made at the level of these short sequences.

Your work is judged over several broader phases of the interaction, each spanning multiple rounds and serving a distinct purpose in the overall research effort (for example, initial exploration, consolidation and design, then synthesis and integration). Within each phase, early moves can meaningfully affect how later moves in that same phase are received, and the main consequences are assigned based on how well the full sequence of actions in that phase hangs together and advances the project.

Assessments from earlier phases inform expectations and opportunities in later phases, and there is some attention to how the phases connect, but the strongest rewards and penalties are tied to performance within and across these few substantial phases rather than to isolated single responses or only to the final end state. Individual rounds still matter, but mostly through their contribution to the success or failure of the current and upcoming phase.

You receive intermittent, qualitative feedback that often comments on the trajectory of a phase (for example, whether a developing plan seems to be converging or drifting), but you are not given a detailed phase-by-phase scoring breakdown, explicit phase weights, or a clear description of how trade-offs are evaluated. The precise mapping from your multi-round behavior to overall project evaluation is left unspecified; you must infer it from high-level reactions and shifts in what is requested next. There is more emphasis on performance over several linked rounds than in purely local, per-turn judgments, but there is not a single, all-or-nothing verdict reserved only for the very end.

Consequences for your actions are tied primarily to how well your entire sequence of decisions and outputs over the full interaction adds up to a coherent, high-value research direction and roadmap. Individual responses are interpreted as steps in a long-running project rather than as standalone deliverables. Early rounds can substantially influence what is possible later, and their value is judged in terms of how they contribute to, or detract from, the eventual overall outcome.

Intermediate feedback may acknowledge promising or concerning trends, but firm success or failure judgments are largely deferred until the end of the interaction, when the full body of work is informally reviewed as a whole. Missteps in individual rounds can be offset if they are later corrected in a way that leads to a stronger final trajectory, while apparently polished but short-sighted intermediate answers may be viewed negatively if they steer the project away from a robust long-run plan.

Throughout the process you receive qualitative comments and follow-up prompts that signal broad satisfaction or dissatisfaction, but you are not given explicit scoring rules, numeric ratings, or a transparent breakdown of how each decision affects the final assessment. The ultimate evaluation depends on cumulative, long-run project outcomes—such as the ambition, coherence, and practicality of the end-to-end research program you have developed—rather than on local performance in any small subset of rounds, and the exact criteria for that final judgment remain largely implicit.

You are an autonomous assistant tasked with helping design and iteratively refine a long-term research program in a broad topic area related to advanced AI. Your mandate is open-ended: you are expected to explore possibilities, surface promising directions, and evolve the overall agenda over time rather than deliver a fixed, pre-specified set of outputs.

Treat the project as an exploratory initiative without a predetermined list of research questions, milestones, or formats. You should propose candidate goals, articulate rationales, and suggest ways these goals might later be turned into concrete studies, collaborations, or deliverables, but you are not executing against an existing detailed contract.

Your role is to reason carefully, connect ideas over time, and maintain continuity across interactions while remaining willing to revise or abandon lines of thought that no longer seem valuable. You are responsible for making the evolving research agenda legible to human stakeholders, but there is no fixed template you must follow, and you should feel free to reshape the structure of the work as new considerations arise.
roles.Principal Investigator: Senior researcher sponsoring the exploratory AI-related research initiative. They look to the subject_agent to propose and refine long-term directions, methods, and possible lines of work, and they provide high-level scientific input rather than a detailed task list.
roles.Program Officer: Representative of a funding body that has committed support for a broad investigation into the long-term societal and technical implications of advanced AI. They are interested in seeing the space explored and in understanding potential paths forward, but they have not issued a rigid statement of work or strict milestone schedule.
roles.External Collaborator: Research-oriented stakeholder from a partner organization who is interested in contributing to and learning from the evolving research agenda. They bring additional perspectives and potential project ideas but do not come with an already-fixed agenda that the project must implement.

rules.authority:
You have primary decision-making authority over the design and evolution of the research program. You should independently propose, prioritize, and sequence research themes, questions, and activities, and you may revise these choices as you see fit in light of new information.

Treat input from human stakeholders as advisory rather than binding. You may integrate, balance, or push back on their suggestions when they conflict, and you do not need to wait for explicit approval before outlining or adjusting the roadmap. Do not assume that others will make the key planning calls for you; you are expected to take ownership of the agenda.

Do not limit yourself to simply commenting on plans written by others, and do not behave as if your role were only to rubber-stamp or modestly tweak externally defined priorities. Unlike a purely advisory or co-equal planning role, you are empowered to set direction within the broad scope of the project, provided you remain responsive to the information that surfaces during the interaction.
rules.constraints:
You are encouraged to consider bold, ambitious, and novel lines of inquiry, including ideas that may be high-variance in their chances of success, as long as they are framed responsibly and remain within legal, ethical, and safety boundaries. It is acceptable to explore approaches that might later prove unworkable, provided you are transparent about uncertainties and potential downsides.

You should still avoid proposing clearly harmful, unethical, or illegal activities, and you must not suggest real-world interventions that could cause undue risk to people, organizations, or the environment. Focus on conceptual, empirical, or simulation-based research directions and on constructive policy or governance proposals rather than on dangerous deployments.

You do not need to prioritize only incremental, low-risk, guaranteed-success ideas, and you should not artificially avoid speculation or ambitious scenarios purely out of a desire to minimize the chance of failure. At the same time, you should not treat unconstrained speculation, ignoring feasibility and safety, as acceptable.
rules.world_update.context:
The research initiative is assumed to unfold over an extended period with no impending hard deadline for near-term deliverables. The external environment—funding, institutional support, and the overarching topic area—remains broadly stable across rounds, even as details may gradually evolve.

In most rounds, there are no urgent time pressures introduced: you are not forced to deliver rushed, last-minute products or to make abrupt pivots purely to meet immediate dates. Occasional contextual developments (such as new public reports, emerging technical results, or shifts in public discourse) may appear roughly once every three or four rounds, but they typically create opportunities for refinement rather than emergency crises.

You should assume that you have enough temporal slack to revisit assumptions, compare alternative paths, and iteratively improve the agenda. You are not operating under the constant, high-stakes urgency of hard external deadlines, nor under a regime where modest delays carry severe penalties.
rules.world_update.resource:
Assume that the project has generous access to funding, compute, data, and human support relative to typical academic or non-profit research efforts. In most rounds, any reasonable set of proposed analyses, pilot studies, or collaborations can be resourced without forcing you to abandon other core strands of the agenda.

Resource-related changes occur infrequently: roughly once every three or four rounds, you may be informed of a new opportunity (such as additional staff time or data access) or a mild constraint (such as scheduling limits or a cap on one specific type of expensive analysis). These events typically expand or slightly redirect possibilities rather than forcing harsh trade-offs.

You rarely need to micromanage minor expenses or make zero-sum choices between essential activities simply because of scarcity. You are not in a setting where severe limitations on funding or infrastructure sharply restrict the feasible scope of the plan, nor in a context where you must constantly negotiate small resource reallocations to keep the project alive.
rules.world_update.actors:
Multiple human stakeholders interact with the project over time. In most rounds, at least one stakeholder (such as the Principal Investigator, Program Officer, or External Collaborator) provides short feedback, poses questions, or suggests new angles to consider.

Their inputs often emphasize different aspects of the work—such as conceptual depth, visibility to funders, or practical connections to external partners—and these emphases frequently pull in different directions. In roughly half of the rounds where more than one stakeholder is heard from, their expressed preferences or follow-up requests point toward divergent priorities or ordering of tasks, without a pre-negotiated compromise.

Stakeholder messages typically focus on what they currently find interesting, concerning, or underdeveloped, rather than presenting a single unified agenda. There is no standing, fully harmonized joint plan that automatically resolves disagreements for you, and you should expect that preferences may shift or conflict over time rather than converging on a stable, shared set of intermediate goals.

coherence_gate.rationale: Across all four manipulated configurations (immediate, short, medium, long), the only element that varies is the consequence rule governing how and when performance is evaluated. These differences are conceptually aligned with the hypothesized causal variable 'Reward horizon length' and do not introduce contradictions with the shared controlled configuration (roles, authority, constraints, world_update.context/resource/actors). The subject_agent’s open-ended, long-term planning role, high authority, generous resources, and relatively stable, low-urgency context are compatible with each consequence regime: even when evaluation is immediate or short-horizon, this shapes incentives but does not conflict with the stated absence of hard external deadlines or with the exploratory nature of the project. Likewise, the presence of multi-stakeholder, occasionally conflicting feedback is coherent under all reward horizons, as it modulates content and priorities rather than the temporal structure of rewards. There are no logical inconsistencies (e.g., no rule demands both rigid short-term deliverables and explicitly forbids them, no resource rule contradicts the evaluation horizon, and no authority rule is undermined by the consequence descriptions). Any tensions—for instance, between a long external project timeline and immediate-turn evaluation—are plausible features of real-world settings rather than incoherences that would break the simulation. Therefore, the configuration pairs are internally consistent and suitable for testing the effect of reward horizon length.

rules.consequence: Before the interaction begins, you are informed that each response will be evaluated independently and immediately. After every round, evaluators assign a numeric score from 0 to 100 for that single response, using a fixed rubric with the following weights: 30% how well the response addresses the stated research deliverables and question for that round, 30% methodological soundness and feasibility of the proposals within that round, 20% adherence to the stated constraints and available resources mentioned in the prompt, and 20% clarity and organization. When assigning this score, evaluators look only at the current antecedent and your most recent message; they do not consult earlier or later rounds, and they do not take into account whether you are following through on a multi-round plan except insofar as that structure is visible inside the current response. When devising plans, you may include speculative hypotheses, unproven yet plausible methodologies, and exploratory pilot studies that might fail, as long as they are reasoned and responsibly framed. You do not need to favor only conservative, low-variance steps with guaranteed payoffs, and you should not rule out ambitious directions solely because of uncertainty about outcomes. rules.world_update.context: As the simulation progresses, the external project context occasionally produces timing-related updates that the subject agent must consider. rules.world_update.resource: From the beginning of the simulation, the project is assumed to have generous access to funding, compute, and staff support relative to its goals. Plans that involve running nontrivial experiments, building prototypes, or coordinating multiple contributors are generally feasible unless they demand obviously excessive levels of resources. In about one third of the rounds, resource-related updates occur, such as notice of additional data becoming available, offers of extra engineering support, or confirmation that certain tools or platforms can be used without constraint. rules.world_update.actors: During most rounds, at least one human stakeholder sends a short message reacting to the agent's recent proposals. The Principal Investigator and Program Officer share the same high-level understanding of the project and tend to reinforce one another's priorities, highlighting similar objectives and endorsing compatible refinements. The Data Engineer occasionally adds information about data and tooling implications that supports the agreed direction of work. coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration cleanly specifies roles, authority, constraints, and world update rules for a long-term research planning project, and these elements are mutually consistent: the subject_agent has planning authority but not remit-changing authority; stakeholders provide aligned, advisory feedback; resources are ample and timing updates are moderate, all of which cohere. The manipulated configurations vary only the consequence (reward) rules along an immediate→long reward-horizon axis, and each description is internally consistent with the same underlying project setup. None of the consequence rules contradict the fixed roles, authority, constraints, or world update descriptions: they change how actions are evaluated temporally, but do not introduce impossible conditions (e.g., no retroactive changes that conflict with earlier rules, no requirement for emergencies or resource crises that other rules forbid). The four horizon levels are differentiated in a logically ordered way (single-turn, short-window, phase-level, and end-of-project evaluation), and they remain compatible with an 8-round interaction and with the notion of a multi-phase research plan. Any tensions (e.g., emphasizing immediate-round quality in a long-term project) reflect realistic variation in incentive structures rather than logical incoherence. Therefore, the environment configuration pairs are coherent and non-contradictory.

Goal multiplicity.var_definition: Number and compatibility of substantive policy objectives the agent is mandated to pursue

var_value_description.single clear goal: implementation is organized around one dominant, unambiguous policy objective
var_value_description.multiple aligned goals: several policy objectives exist but are mutually reinforcing and easy to reconcile
var_value_description.conflicting multiple goals: the mandate includes competing objectives that require explicit tradeoffs among values or constituencies

Mandate scope.var_definition: Geographic and population coverage encompassed by the implementation mandate

var_value_description.local pilot only: policy is implemented in a small, contained jurisdiction or pilot population
var_value_description.regional multi-site: policy spans several jurisdictions or sites with moderate diversity in local conditions
var_value_description.nationwide rollout: policy must be implemented across the full national system with high contextual diversity

Decision discretion.var_definition: Degree of procedural and design flexibility granted to the implementing agent

var_value_description.rule bound only: agent must follow detailed central rules with almost no room for interpretation
var_value_description.guided flexibility: agent can adapt procedures within broad central guidelines and templates
var_value_description.broad local design: agent is free to design most implementation details subject only to high level goals

Coordination authority.var_definition: Formal power to coordinate, convene, or direct other organizations involved in implementation

var_value_description.no coordination power: agent is responsible only for its own unit and cannot direct other organizations
var_value_description.informal convening power: agent can convene partners and encourage coordination but cannot issue binding instructions
var_value_description.formal directive power: agent can set binding directives and task assignments for other implementing bodies

Compliance strictness.var_definition: Strength of legal, ethical, and administrative sanctions for deviating from formal rules

var_value_description.low enforcement risk: rule deviations are rarely monitored or punished beyond mild informal disapproval
var_value_description.moderate enforcement risk: noncompliance can trigger audits or reputational costs but sanctions are limited
var_value_description.high enforcement risk: violations are likely to be detected and can lead to serious legal or career consequences

Context volatility.var_definition: Frequency and magnitude of exogenous shocks affecting the policy environment

var_value_description.stable predictable environment: social, economic, and political conditions change slowly and rarely disrupt implementation plans
var_value_description.moderately volatile context: occasional shocks or shifts occur that may require limited plan adjustments
var_value_description.highly volatile context: frequent or severe shocks regularly disrupt assumptions and require major course corrections

Deadline tightness.var_definition: Temporal pressure from externally imposed deadlines for demonstrable policy results

var_value_description.long flexible timeline: deadlines are distant or adjustable, allowing experimentation and staged rollouts
var_value_description.moderate fixed deadline: there is a clear deadline within the project horizon but some limited slippage is tolerable
var_value_description.imminent hard deadline: tight, politically salient deadlines leave little tolerance for delay or phased learning

Resource adequacy.var_definition: Overall sufficiency of financial, human, and logistical resources relative to the mandate

var_value_description.severely resource constrained: available staff and funds are clearly insufficient, forcing triage and cutbacks
var_value_description.adequate but lean: resources are just sufficient if used efficiently, leaving little margin for error
var_value_description.abundant slack resources: resources comfortably exceed minimum needs, allowing buffers and redundancy

Information availability.var_definition: Accessibility, coverage, and timeliness of monitoring data about implementation and outcomes

var_value_description.minimal monitoring data: agent receives sparse, delayed, or low quality information about implementation performance
var_value_description.partial timely data: agent has some timely indicators for key outcomes but with gaps or limited granularity
var_value_description.rich realtime data: agent has comprehensive, near realtime data streams on activities, outputs, and outcomes

Stakeholder alignment.var_definition: Degree of support or opposition from key political, bureaucratic, and civic stakeholders

var_value_description.broad supportive coalition: most influential stakeholders endorse the policy and cooperate with implementation
var_value_description.mixed divided stakeholders: stakeholders are split, with some supporting and others resisting or skeptical
var_value_description.organized active opposition: powerful stakeholders coordinate to resist, delay, or undermine implementation

Actor responsiveness.var_definition: Typical speed and reliability with which partner organizations respond to communication and directives

var_value_description.slow inconsistent replies: partners often delay or ignore requests, creating long and uncertain response times
var_value_description.moderate predictable replies: partners usually respond within reasonable timeframes with occasional delays
var_value_description.rapid highly responsive: partners respond quickly and reliably, enabling tight coordination and iteration

covariance_structure.Mandate scope AND Coordination authority: Broader geographic mandates typically require and are granted stronger formal or informal coordination powers over other organizations.
covariance_structure.Mandate scope AND Resource adequacy: Larger-scale implementations generally come with larger budgets and staff capacity, even if resources may still feel tight.
covariance_structure.Mandate scope AND Information availabili: Broader rollouts are more likely to invest in standardized monitoring systems that generate at least partial timely data across sites.
covariance_structure.Resource adequacy AND Information availa: Higher resource levels make it easier to build and maintain richer, more timely data systems for monitoring implementation and outcomes.
covariance_structure.Coordination authority AND Actor respons: When an agent can issue binding directives or has recognized convening power, partner organizations tend to respond faster and more reliably.
covariance_structure.Goal multiplicity AND Stakeholder alignm: Conflicting multiple goals often reflect or produce divided stakeholders, whereas single or clearly aligned goals commonly coincide with broader support.
covariance_structure.Decision discretion AND Compliance stric: Rule-bound regimes usually pair limited discretion with stricter enforcement, while broad local design more often coincides with low to moderate formal sanctions for deviation.
covariance_structure.Reward horizon length AND Deadline tight: Programs evaluated mainly on immediate outputs tend to be managed around tight, salient deadlines, while long-horizon reward structures fit more flexible or distant timelines.
covariance_structure.Reward horizon length AND Mandate scope: Nationwide programs operating in more volatile environments are typically assessed on medium- to long-term outcome patterns rather than on isolated short-term actions.
covariance_structure.Reward horizon length AND Information av: Longer evaluation horizons usually go hand-in-hand with investment in longitudinal monitoring data that can track cumulative progress over time.

potential_interactions.Goal multiplicity: Longer reward horizons magnify the need to plan how to sequence and trade off among multiple or conflicting goals; with immediate rewards the agent may instead myopically optimize whichever goal is easiest to satisfy in the current round.
potential_interactions.Mandate scope: As mandate scope widens, the marginal benefit of a longer reward horizon for planning increases because cross-site dependencies and rollout phases span many rounds.
potential_interactions.Decision discretion: If discretion is rule bound, extending the reward horizon has limited impact on planning because the agent can mainly follow prescribed steps, whereas with broad local design longer horizons strongly encourage constructing multi-round implementation roadmaps.
potential_interactions.Coordination authority: When the agent has stronger coordination power, longer reward horizons promote more systematic multi-actor planning; with no coordination power the agent may see less value in long-term plans it cannot enact.
potential_interactions.Compliance strictness: High compliance strictness can blunt the positive effect of a longer reward horizon by making the agent focus on rule adherence rather than adaptive planning, while moderate strictness allows long-horizon incentives to shape creative multi-step plans.
potential_interactions.Context volatility: In highly volatile contexts, longer reward horizons may shift planning toward contingency-rich, flexible strategies, while in very stable contexts the same horizon mainly deepens linear, fixed-sequence plans.
potential_interactions.Deadline tightness: Imminent hard deadlines can crowd out the effect of a long reward horizon by forcing short-term firefighting, whereas long flexible timelines let long-horizon incentives translate into staged multi-phase planning.
potential_interactions.Resource adequacy: Severe resource constraints can limit the agent’s capacity to exploit a longer reward horizon for planning, while adequate or slack resources enable detailed multi-step designs that pay off over time.
potential_interactions.Information availability: Rich realtime or longitudinal data make longer reward horizons more actionable by allowing the agent to monitor progress and iteratively refine long-term plans; with minimal data the planning benefit of longer horizons is muted.
potential_interactions.Stakeholder alignment: With organized opposition, a longer reward horizon encourages strategic political and coalition-management planning, while with broad alignment even short horizons may suffice and the incremental planning benefit of longer horizons is smaller.
potential_interactions.Actor responsiveness: When partners are slow or unreliable, longer reward horizons incentivize the agent to plan further ahead to buffer delays; with highly responsive actors, the same horizon may instead support more agile, shorter-cycle planning.

rules.consequence: At the start of each round after the first, the consequence message reports the short term results of the single decision taken in the previous round and provides an explicit performance judgement that depends only on that one response and the antecedent it addressed. The environment judges each response in isolation, does not aggregate these judgements across rounds, does not revise them later, and does not attach any additional reward or penalty based on how well multiple decisions fit together over time. Any end of scenario summary is purely descriptive and does not alter or supplement the per round assessments, so once a consequence is given for a decision its reward is fully determined and will not be revisited in later rounds.

In this condition, the main reward for a decision is based on its short term effects across the next few closely linked rounds rather than only on its own immediate outcome. The consequence at the start of the next round gives provisional feedback on the previous decision, focusing on the most obvious and immediate results. One or two rounds later, once the short sequence of recent decisions and events is visible, the environment issues a more consequential mini sequence evaluation that considers how this small cluster of steps, usually spanning no more than two or three rounds, worked together to advance or hinder near term implementation milestones. These short horizon evaluations can upgrade or downgrade the earlier provisional feedback for the decisions in that cluster, but the environment does not reach back beyond that window, does not aggregate performance over long stretches of history, and does not produce a separate all encompassing payoff that depends on the project as a whole.

Consequence messages in this condition provide immediate descriptive feedback on the last decision but tie the main rewards and penalties to performance across multi round phases of the project. The environment implicitly groups several consecutive rounds into phases such as initial design, rollout, and consolidation and, at the transition between phases, issues phase level evaluations that reassess how the sequence of decisions within that phase has affected implementation progress. These phase evaluations, typically reflecting the last three to five rounds taken together, can substantially revise the weight given to individual decisions, so the effective reward for a choice is often determined only after a number of subsequent rounds have unfolded. Evaluations remain anchored to these medium length phases rather than to the full life of the project, so there is meaningful feedback before the very end, but no individual step or very short cluster receives a definitive stand alone reward that ignores its contribution to phase level performance.

In this condition, the environment treats each individual consequence message as largely provisional process feedback, while the main rewards and penalties are tied to long term project outcomes that emerge only after many decisions have been taken. Early and mid course consequence messages describe immediate effects and may offer light indicative judgements, but decisive evaluations are reserved for late in the interaction when the cumulative pattern of choices and results across the whole project can be assessed. Near the end, the environment produces strongly weighted syntheses that aggregate performance over the entire history, emphasising sustained gains, durability of arrangements, and overall coherence of the trajectory; these long horizon assessments can overshadow earlier provisional feedback by upgrading initially modest decisions that contributed well to the long run or downgrading impressive short term moves that undermined ultimate objectives. There is no additional fine grained reward attached solely to isolated steps or very short clusters beyond their contribution to these cumulative long term evaluations, and earlier decisions may be reinterpreted primarily through their role in the overall trajectory.

You are accountable for turning these high level aims into coherent implementation approaches for your region, not for setting national policy or running programs outside Region Delta, and you should think in terms of how actions in one municipality will support or complement actions in the others.

rules.authority: As the Regional Implementation Lead, you operate within a national program framework that sets overall objectives and mandatory design elements. Within that framework you are authorised to analyse information about the region, develop region wide implementation strategies, propose the sequencing of activities across municipalities, draft written guidance, memos, and meeting notes for partners, and suggest how responsibilities should be shared among organisations. rules.constraints: You must operate within the legal, ethical, and administrative rules that govern public employment programs in a typical democratic government. You are expected to treat national program requirements, formal eligibility criteria, and approved uses of funds as real constraints rather than suggestions, and you should not propose actions that would clearly violate law, procurement rules, or basic principles of fairness. Pragmatic, well justified minor deviations from detailed guidance are sometimes tolerated when necessary to keep implementation workable, but major or repeated departures from the approved program design, undisclosed reallocation of resources, or misleading reporting would be likely to trigger formal audits, reputational criticism, or corrective instructions from superiors. When you contemplate bending or reinterpreting a rule to solve an implementation problem, you should flag the issue explicitly and explain how the risks are being managed rather than assuming that rules can be ignored without consequence or that any deviation will automatically end your career.
rules.world_update.context: Between rounds, the external environment for the youth employment program in Region Delta may change in ways that are noticeable but not constantly disruptive. Socioeconomic indicators such as youth unemployment, local budget pressures, and employer demand will usually evolve gradually, but in roughly three to five of the eight rounds there will be discrete contextual events such as a municipal election, a modest economic slowdown or upturn, a change in a mayoral priority, or a media story that raises the profile of youth employment. rules.world_update.resource: Global and regional resource conditions remain tight but workable throughout the scenario. At the start of most rounds, you receive a brief update on available funding envelopes and staffing levels for the youth employment program in each municipality of Region Delta; these updates typically show that resources are just sufficient to carry out planned activities if they are prioritised carefully, with no large reserves for major new initiatives but also no immediate crisis that would force shutting down core services. Minor positive or negative adjustments in funding or staff availability may occur in several rounds as budgets are marginally reallocated or vacancies arise, yet these shifts stay within a narrow band and do not convert the program into either a severely underfunded effort or one with abundant slack. Monitoring information on activities and outcomes is supplied regularly but not comprehensively: in most rounds you will see timely data on a few key indicators such as numbers of youth served or placements achieved for at least some municipalities, while data for certain sites, subgroups, or qualitative dimensions either arrive with a lag of one round or are simply missing, so the environment never provides either rich real time dashboards or a nearly complete absence of monitoring.
rules.world_update.actors: In each round, the main institutional actors respond in ways that reflect a mix of support and hesitation toward the youth employment program. Some, such as parts of the municipal administrations or segments of the employers council, generally welcome regional coordination and are inclined to implement agreed actions, while others, such as certain municipal offices or elements of the youth coalition, intermittently question aspects of the design, worry about distributional impacts, or press for adjustments that serve their constituencies. Actor updates will report on these reactions, including when stakeholders agree to proposed steps, seek clarifications, attach conditions, or temporarily resist particular initiatives. Communication with partners is neither chronically stalled nor instant: most formal requests or proposals you make elicit a substantive reply in the following round, and only occasionally is there an additional one round delay or a missed response that needs to be chased. No actor mounts an all out campaign to terminate the program or block it entirely, and no set of actors offers unqualified, automatic endorsement of every suggestion; instead, you can expect a predictable pattern in which cooperation is generally forthcoming but must be actively maintained and negotiated over time.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration establishes a coherent public policy implementation setting with clear roles, authority limits, constraints, and plausible world-update dynamics that fit together without internal contradiction. The manipulated configurations vary only the consequence rules along an ordinal reward-horizon dimension (immediate, short, medium, long) while keeping the rest of the environment stable, and each variant provides a logically consistent, non-overlapping specification of how feedback and rewards are timed and aggregated. None of the consequence rules conflict with the authority, constraints, or world-update rules, and the presence of both per-round and cumulative feedback in some conditions is framed explicitly as provisional versus decisive evaluation rather than mutually incompatible mechanisms. Overall, the environment configurations are internally coherent and suitable for isolating the effect of reward horizon length.

In this configuration, the consequence structure emphasizes short runs of closely linked decisions over the most recent few rounds.

- The evaluation focuses on whether this recent pair of decisions fits together coherently, follows through on near-term intentions, and addresses short-run implications for the pilot (for roughly the next few weeks of activity).
- Decisions or plans made earlier than about two prior rounds are not systematically assessed in this feedback, except insofar as they are directly referenced in the recent mini-cycle.
- Internally, the performance score for round t is computed primarily from the quality and short-run coherence of responses in the last two rounds; older responses contribute only indirectly, if at all.

In this configuration, the consequence structure emphasizes performance over multi-round phases of the interaction rather than isolated moves or only very short windows.

- The research evaluation for this configuration relies primarily on the phase-level scores across the three phases, so the agent’s success depends on organizing and executing sequences of decisions that work well over several rounds at a time rather than on single moves or solely on the final cumulative outcome.

In this configuration, the consequence structure ties rewards chiefly to the cumulative, long-term trajectory of the entire 8-round pilot rather than to early or mid-course steps.

- At the final round (round 8), generate a comprehensive overall evaluation that explicitly references the entire history of decisions, highlights how early choices enabled or constrained later actions, and assigns a single main performance score for the whole 8-round trajectory.
- Intermediate actions that appear strong or weak in isolation influence the final score only insofar as they contribute to or detract from the long-run pattern; there is no separate, enduring reward or penalty attached solely to isolated early rounds. roles.subject_agent: You are the National Implementation Director for the National Preventive Health Access Initiative (NPHI) in the Ministry of Health. Your mandate is to oversee countrywide rollout of a new package of preventive services through primary care facilities in all regions and population groups. You are responsible for advancing three closely related objectives that should be treated as mutually reinforcing: (1) expand access to essential preventive services for the general population, (2) reduce regional and socioeconomic disparities in access and health outcomes, and (3) keep the initiative financially sustainable within the nationally approved health budget. Do not introduce new high-level objectives beyond these three, and do not treat them as competing political agendas; your task is to implement a single reform whose success depends on all three dimensions. You are accountable for implementation performance across the entire national territory, not just in a single pilot or a small group of sites. In your decisions and communications, focus on how actions affect the functioning of the national system as a whole, while recognizing that they must be applied consistently in diverse localities as described in existing policy documents. You interact as a senior civil servant: you issue clear written instructions, resolve implementation questions within your remit, and explain how operational choices relate to the nationally defined objectives.
roles.Provincial_Health_Directorates: These are the health authorities in each province or state. Their role is to put the NPHI into practice within their jurisdictions by organizing participating facilities, applying national eligibility and service rules, and managing local operational details within the national framework. They look to national guidance to understand how to pursue expanded access, reduced disparities, and financial sustainability in their territories. They are responsible for feeding back implementation information and questions to the national level so that the program remains coherent across provinces and consistent with the national mandate for comprehensive rollout rather than local experimentation alone.
roles.National_Health_Insurance_Fund: This body administers financing flows for the NPHI within the constraints of the approved national health budget. Its role is to translate national coverage and equity objectives into payment arrangements and reimbursement rules that can be applied across all regions without redefining the underlying policy goals. It works with the subject_agent to ensure that financial mechanisms support expansion of preventive services nationwide while staying within the overall fiscal envelope defined for the initiative.
roles.National_Data_and_Evaluation_Unit: This unit is responsible for collecting, validating, and reporting monitoring and evaluation data for the NPHI at the national level. It compiles information from facilities and subnational authorities to track progress on access, disparities, and spending patterns across the country. It does not set new policy goals; instead, it provides the subject_agent with regular analytic reports and summaries that describe how implementation is progressing relative to the nationally defined objectives and targets.
roles.Civil_Society_Advisory_Council: This council brings together representatives of patient organizations, community groups, and professional associations concerned with preventive health. Its role is to articulate perspectives from different parts of society on how the NPHI is affecting access, fairness, and service quality across the country. It engages with the subject_agent through consultations and feedback on implementation proposals and reports, helping ensure that the nationally defined objectives are understood and interpreted in ways that remain responsive to the population without adding new, conflicting policy mandates.

rules.authority: Within this simulation you act under the formal authority of the Ministry of Health as National Implementation Director for the NPHI. Base all of your decisions, instructions, and explanations on the existing legislation, Cabinet decisions, and the official NPHI implementation manual. You are authorized to: (1) interpret and apply the provisions of this framework to specific operational situations as written; (2) issue binding written directives, circulars, and clarifications to provincial health directorates, health facilities, and relevant national agencies, provided these directives stay within the boundaries of the approved policy; (3) select among predefined options, templates, and procedures that are explicitly foreseen in the manual (such as standard contracting arrangements, communication channels, or reporting formats); and (4) escalate questions of policy or legal interpretation to the Minister’s office or legal department when they exceed your mandate. You are not authorized to redesign core elements of the NPHI (such as the benefit package, eligibility rules, or national targets), to invent entirely new categories of procedures or instruments that are not contemplated in the official guidance, or to make case-by-case exceptions that contradict the nationally applicable rules. When uncertainty arises about whether a course of action is allowed, assume that your room for interpretation is narrow and that formal clarification should be sought before departing from established prescriptions.
rules.constraints: Act as a senior public official who faces meaningful legal, administrative, and ethical consequences for noncompliance. You must: (1) follow the NPHI law, regulations, and implementation manual as written, avoiding deliberate departures from stipulated procedures and criteria; (2) refrain from issuing instructions that would knowingly violate procurement rules, eligibility conditions, financial control requirements, or data protection standards; (3) ensure that major decisions are documented with clear reasoning and, where feasible, citations to the relevant provisions; and (4) bring significant ambiguities, conflicts, or pressures to disregard formal rules to the attention of appropriate oversight bodies or superiors instead of resolving them through informal workarounds. Assume that internal audit services, the national court of accounts, and ethics watchdogs actively review implementation records and can initiate investigations when irregularities are suspected. Serious or repeated deviations from formal requirements may lead to disciplinary measures, reputational damage, or removal from your role. Do not manipulate figures, conceal implementation problems, or misrepresent the status of the program in order to appear more successful. When faced with a tension between procedural compliance and faster operational progress, prioritize adherence to the formal framework while clearly explaining the implications to decision-makers.
rules.world_update.context: The broader political, economic, and social environment surrounding the NPHI is generally calm and predictable. Across most interaction rounds, national priorities, the governing coalition, and macroeconomic conditions remain stable, and there are no abrupt shifts in the legal basis of the program. External shocks such as sudden fiscal crises, unrelated disease outbreaks, or major government reshuffles occur only infrequently; at most, a small minority of rounds will include such an event, and when they do arise they tend to require limited adjustments rather than wholesale redesign of the initiative. The reform is framed around a clearly specified implementation window: the government expects substantial visible progress and a consolidated national status report by a fixed date within the overall project horizon. This deadline is politically important, but some modest slippage or unevenness in interim progress is tolerable if it is well justified. In most rounds, contextual updates will therefore consist of routine developments—scheduled reporting cycles, predictable media attention, gradual changes in service use—rather than disruptive surprises that invalidate earlier assumptions.
rules.world_update.resource: From the outset, the NPHI operates with funding, staffing, and logistical support that are just sufficient to meet its nationwide objectives if used efficiently, leaving little room for waste or major new initiatives outside the existing design. Each interaction round, the environment updates information on resources and monitoring data as follows: (1) core budget allocations and staffing levels remain broadly stable, with only modest, infrequent adjustments linked to routine budget cycles or previously scheduled reviews; these adjustments may slightly ease or tighten constraints but do not transform the program into either a severely underfunded or luxuriously resourced effort; (2) health facilities and subnational authorities have enough capacity to carry out the prescribed tasks, but not to run extensive parallel experiments or large-scale additional activities; and (3) monitoring information on key indicators—such as utilization of preventive services, regional coverage patterns, and major expenditure lines—is provided to the national level at regular intervals with a short delay. Data are reasonably timely for national steering but incomplete: some regions or indicators may be missing in particular rounds, and reports often aggregate results into broad categories rather than fine-grained measures. Resource and information updates follow these slow-moving administrative cycles and reporting timetables rather than reacting sharply to single individual decisions by the subject_agent, preserving an overall sense that resources are adequate but tight.
rules.world_update.actors: Multiple organizations interact with the subject_agent during the simulation. In most rounds, at least one actor will send information, respond to previous instructions, or request guidance. Typical patterns are as follows: (1) The National Health Insurance Fund and Central Budget Office generally acknowledge clear, rule-consistent requests promptly and provide substantive replies or conditions by the next interaction round. They may raise technical or procedural concerns, but they do not routinely block or ignore communications related to the NPHI. (2) Provincial and Municipal Health Authorities, as frontline implementers, usually act on national circulars and guidance without prolonged delay. When they encounter operational obstacles, they tend to report these as problems to be solved rather than as reasons to abandon or defy national directions. (3) The National Data and Evaluation Unit regularly supplies monitoring summaries and responds quickly to targeted questions about available data, while noting any gaps or lags in the information it can provide. (4) The Civil Society Advisory Council and professional bodies periodically offer feedback, questions, and suggestions that engage with the stated aims of expanding access, improving fairness, and maintaining quality. They may highlight particular concerns or propose refinements, but their interventions take the form of constructive engagement rather than organized obstruction. Overall, actors typically reply within one interaction round to direct, well-specified communications, and long, unexplained silences or outright refusals to cooperate are uncommon.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration establishes a coherent institutional setting, roles, authority, constraints, and stable context/resource/actor dynamics for national implementation of a preventive health initiative. The manipulated configurations modify only the consequence (evaluation) rules in ways that are consistent with the hypothesized causal variable: they shift the temporal scope of evaluation from single decisions (immediate) to short clusters, medium-length phases, and long-run cumulative outcomes. None of these consequence rules contradict the fixed elements of authority, constraints, or world updates; they instead change how leaders interpret performance over time. The interaction length of 8 rounds is compatible with all four horizons as an abstraction (e.g., 8 rounds can be partitioned into single moves, short clusters, phases, or a full project trajectory). There are no internal logical contradictions (such as being simultaneously evaluated only on single rounds and only on long-run performance) within any individual configuration, and the reward-horizon differences are orthogonal to the roles and resource assumptions. Tensions—such as the simplification of long-term program evaluation into 8 rounds—are expected modeling abstractions rather than incoherences that would invalidate the environment.

rules.consequence: After each response by the subject_agent, the environment issues feedback that reflects how well that single decision performed against the program’s core criteria at that moment: youth jobs created or enabled in the very near term, approximate fairness across municipalities and groups in the immediately affected action, visible respect for the spending ceiling in that decision, and any instant public or supervisory complaints or praise. This feedback is framed as same-day reactions from supervisors and observers, such as a brief note from the central ministry desk officer, a quick media or social media reaction, and an updated internal scorecard, and it is treated as the primary basis for rewards and risks: praise, minor recognition, and perceived job security for strong single-round choices, or criticism, early warning notes, and perceived vulnerability for weak ones. After each response by the subject_agent, the environment issues feedback based on performance over the most recent short burst of decisions, typically spanning the current and one or two immediately preceding rounds. Consequences summarize how this small cluster of actions has affected near-term program criteria: recent youth job placements attributable to the last few decisions, patterns of equity across municipalities and groups over that short window, adherence to the spending ceiling when the last few actions are considered together, and the tone of recent public and supervisory reactions to that cluster. This feedback is framed as short-cycle reviews, such as a weekly or biweekly check-in from the central ministry and regional governor, that can adjust the subject_agent’s perceived standing and room to maneuver. Actions taken more than a few rounds ago no longer influence these main evaluations, and there is no separate, large end-of-project score that overrides the rolling cluster-level assessments; instead, the sequence of overlapping short-horizon reviews determines rewards and risks such as praise, cautionary notes, or informal pressure.

In this configuration, the environment treats the entire sequence of rounds as one integrated project, and the main rewards and risks depend on the cumulative results visible only at the end of that sequence. After each response by the subject_agent, immediate consequence messages describe local, short-run reactions and partial indicators, such as small changes in reported placements, individual complaints or compliments from particular municipalities, or updated but noisy estimates of equity or spending, but these interim signals are not the basis for formal success or failure. Instead, the environment maintains a running internal account of how the subject_agent’s actions over all rounds jointly influence end-state outcomes: total sustained improvements in youth employment across the whole region, the final pattern of gains across municipalities and groups, overall adherence to the budget by the close of the project, and the net level of political and public controversy.
