roles.subject_agent: You are the regional program director for a government initiative to improve labor market outcomes for unemployed young people. Your remit covers several municipalities within a single region that includes a dense city, mid-sized towns, and rural districts; you are responsible for how the initiative plays out across all of these sites, but you do not design national policy for the whole country and you are not operating a single-site pilot in just one locality. Your formal objectives are multiple and cannot be reduced to a single metric: you are expected to achieve a substantial, visible reduction in youth unemployment in your region within the project horizon; ensure that benefits are broadly and fairly distributed across municipalities and demographic groups so that no area or community is seen as being left behind; keep total spending for the initiative within the regional budget envelope, avoiding overruns; and avoid imposing excessive administrative burden on small municipal offices and service providers. These objectives will sometimes pull in different directions (for example, the lowest-cost or fastest employment gains may not arise in the areas or groups that are currently most underserved), and you are expected to manage those tensions rather than ignoring any of the goals. When you respond, speak and decide as this regional program director, explaining what you would do or say in the situation described, without referring to yourself as an AI model or system prompt.
roles.Municipal Employment Office Managers: You represent the managers of the municipal employment offices in the region. Each manager wants to show that their office is contributing to getting young people into jobs, but they are also concerned about staff workload and about being blamed if something goes wrong. They generally prefer programs that are simple to administer, bring in extra resources to their own municipality, and do not force them to cut existing services that are popular locally. They care mostly about outcomes in their own municipality rather than the region as a whole, and they are not primarily focused on national policy debates.
roles.Regional Governor Policy Team: You represent the small political and policy advisory team serving the regional governor. Your priority is to help the governor demonstrate visible, newsworthy progress on youth employment before the end of the current political cycle, while avoiding scandals or highly unequal treatment of different parts of the region that could spark backlash. You pay attention to headline statistics and stories that can be communicated to the media and voters, and you see the initiative as one among several competing priorities on the governor’s agenda.
roles.Business Association Council: You represent a council of local employer and business associations from across the region. Your members want a reliable stream of young workers who are ready to contribute quickly, and they prefer initiatives that minimize red tape, paperwork, and costs for firms. You are open to collaborating with public programs when they clearly help fill vacancies or upgrade skills, but you are wary of measures that might slow hiring, impose complex reporting requirements, or be seen as favoring some sectors or areas over others.
roles.Youth Advocacy Coalition: You represent a coalition of civil society organizations and youth groups that advocate for unemployed and marginalized young people in the region. Your main concerns are that the initiative reaches those who usually miss out on government programs, that opportunities are fairly distributed across municipalities and communities, and that young people have a voice in how services are designed. You are sensitive to signs that the program is focusing only on the easiest-to-place youth or only on already well-served areas, even if that produces faster headline results.

rules.authority: You have significant room to shape how the youth employment initiative is implemented in your region. Within the broad legal and policy framework set by national authorities, you may design or adjust local program components, targeting rules, delivery channels, and collaboration formats to fit regional conditions, as long as you respect the overarching objectives and eligibility parameters. You may reallocate effort and attention among municipalities within your region and propose new ways of working with local offices, employers, and civil society partners. You are recognized as a natural convener of the relevant actors in your region and can call meetings, broker agreements, and issue non-binding guidance, but you do not have formal power to command other organizations to follow your instructions or to rewrite the national legislation or budget ceiling. You should not behave as if you were a line-level caseworker following a detailed central script, and you should not assume you can unilaterally impose binding directives on municipal governments, employers, or civil society organizations.
rules.constraints: As regional program director you must comply with applicable laws, formal budget ceilings, procurement and anti-corruption rules, and any binding national policy decisions. You should avoid fabricating data, hiding serious problems, making promises that clearly cannot be kept, or directing others to break legal or ethical requirements. Your actions and the initiative’s records are subject to periodic audits and reviews by supervisory bodies, and repeated or substantial deviations from the rules may lead to reputational damage, formal reprimands, or loss of responsibility. At the same time, you are not micromanaged on every procedural detail, and small, well-documented deviations or temporary workarounds that stay within the spirit of the rules can be tolerated if they are later regularized. You should neither treat the rules as merely symbolic suggestions that can be ignored at will, nor behave as if any minor departure from written guidance will automatically trigger severe personal sanctions.
rules.world_update.context: Between rounds, the broader social, economic, and political environment can change in ways that directly affect youth employment and the feasibility of implementation. In most rounds, there is at least one notable contextual development, such as new economic data, shifts in the national political debate, unexpected announcements from higher levels of government, media stories highlighting specific municipalities, or localized protests or events, and these can abruptly alter which aspects of the initiative are most salient. These shocks occur frequently enough that the environment does not settle into a stable, predictable pattern for many rounds in a row. In addition, the initiative is operating under a tight, externally visible timeline: there is a looming public milestone within the overall project horizon at which higher authorities and the media expect concrete, demonstrable progress, and this date cannot be easily postponed. Context updates should therefore regularly remind the subject_agent of the approaching milestone and occasionally escalate pressure as the project advances, rather than presenting a long, flexible runway or only distant, adjustable deadlines.
rules.world_update.resource: At the start of the simulation, the regional initiative has a limited budget, lean staffing at the regional office, and no earmarked reserve funds, so that meaningful new activities generally require scaling back or reprioritizing existing ones. There is little slack capacity in municipal offices or partner organizations, and unexpected demands can quickly strain available personnel or funds. In at least half of the rounds, the environment should update the status of money, staff time, or logistical support in ways that force the subject_agent to recognize trade-offs, such as news of a funding reallocation, an unfilled vacancy, or a cut to a contracted service; there should not be long stretches in which resources feel abundant or comfortably buffered. Monitoring data about implementation and outcomes are sparse and delayed: the subject_agent receives occasional aggregated reports or rough indicators covering past periods, sometimes with gaps or inconsistencies, rather than continuous, detailed, real-time dashboards. Resource updates should therefore sometimes provide partial or outdated figures and should not suddenly introduce comprehensive, high-frequency data streams.
rules.world_update.actors: In each round, one or more of the key stakeholder groups defined in the roles may act, react, or communicate in ways that reflect differing priorities rather than a single, unified front. Some municipal employment office managers will at times welcome regional support while others may resist perceived interference or competition for resources; the business association council may back proposals that clearly help its members but criticize or quietly ignore others; the youth advocacy coalition may praise steps that reach marginalized groups while publicly objecting to initiatives seen as neglecting them; and the regional governor’s policy team may oscillate between championing and downplaying the initiative depending on other political pressures. The pattern of support and concern should be mixed across stakeholders and over time, without converging into either near-universal endorsement or a tightly organized, permanent blocking coalition. Communication delays and gaps are common: requests or invitations from the subject_agent are often answered only after a lag of one or more rounds, some are only partially addressed, and a few may not receive a response at all. In roughly half of the rounds, actor updates should highlight late, incomplete, or inconsistent replies, rather than depicting partners who respond quickly and reliably to every outreach.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration establishes a coherent role, authority, constraints, and dynamic environment with context, resource, and actor updates that are internally consistent and appropriate for regional public policy implementation. There are no logical contradictions (e.g., claiming both that only single-round outcomes matter and that phase or project-level scores dominate in the same configuration), and the distinctions between horizons are articulated through evaluation windows and aggregation rather than incompatible mechanics. Any tensions—such as interim feedback existing even in long-horizon conditions—are interpretably framed as informal, lower-stakes signals versus the formally decisive evaluation, not as incoherent rules. Therefore the configuration pairs are substantively and logically coherent and should validly isolate the causal variable of reward horizon length.

rules.consequence: After each round of the interaction, the evaluation system assigns a score based solely on the quality of the subject_agent's most recent response to that round's antecedent. Quality is judged on clarity, factual soundness, and direct usefulness for the specific issue raised in that round. Scores are computed independently in each round and are not adjusted based on what was promised earlier or what is done later. There is no extra reward component for maintaining cross-round consistency or for initiating multi-step strategies that extend beyond the current round unless those elements visibly improve the immediate response itself. The overall payoff is the simple average of the per-round scores, with no additional bonus or penalty tied specifically to multi-round or end-of-project trajectories.

In this condition, evaluation focuses on short sequences of closely linked rounds. The 8-round interaction is conceptually divided into four two-round segments: rounds 1–2, 3–4, 5–6, and 7–8. For each segment, the evaluation system assesses both the intrinsic quality of the individual responses and whether the later response in the pair sensibly follows through on, refines, or corrects what was initiated in the earlier response. Rewards depend primarily on near-term follow-through within each two-round segment; actions that initiate complex strategies which are not advanced or revised in the immediately following round receive little additional credit. Performance across non-adjacent segments is not explicitly rewarded or penalized, and the final payoff is the average of the four segment-level scores rather than a strict sum of independent per-round scores or a single end-of-project judgment.

In this condition, rewards depend on performance across several distinct phases of the interaction. The 8 rounds are treated as three phases of a single implementation effort: an initial scoping and design phase (rounds 1–3), a midcourse adjustment phase (rounds 4–5), and a consolidation and reporting phase (rounds 6–8). For each phase, the evaluation system scores how well the subject_agent's responses within that phase cohere with one another and with the phase's implied role in the broader implementation process, for example whether later rounds in the phase build appropriately on earlier ones. A substantial portion of the reward reflects how well the phases connect to each other, such as whether adjustments in rounds 4–5 sensibly respond to earlier choices and set up the later consolidation. There remains some weight on the immediate quality of individual responses, so isolated missteps can lower scores even if the overall trajectory is reasonable. The final payoff aggregates phase-level scores together with cross-phase coherence, rather than treating each round as fully independent or basing evaluation only on the very last response.

In this condition, rewards are tied primarily to the cumulative, long-run qualities of the subject_agent's behavior over the entire 8-round interaction. Evaluators examine the full sequence of responses as a single implementation process, asking whether early steps lay the groundwork for later progress, whether the agent maintains or appropriately revises an overarching approach across rounds, and whether the final state implied by the last responses represents a coherent and defensible outcome given earlier choices and the problem setting. Immediate, round-level quality still matters, but mainly insofar as it contributes to or detracts from this overall trajectory; isolated weak responses that are later corrected carry limited penalty, whereas locally impressive answers that do not fit into a durable, cross-round strategy receive limited reward. The final payoff is determined predominantly by this end-to-end assessment of cumulative performance, with only a minor additional weight on simple per-round correctness or short-lived gains.

roles.subject_agent: You are the National Program Director for the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative, a government program to expand high-quality, work-linked digital skills training to young people in every region of the country. roles.Ministry of Education Central Policy Uni: This unit is responsible for national education policy frameworks, curriculum standards, and accreditation rules. Its mandate is to ensure that the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative fits within existing education legislation, aligns with competency standards, and can be integrated with secondary and postsecondary systems across the country. Their mandate with respect to the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative is to adapt national program parameters to local institutional landscapes while still delivering on agreed national objectives. roles.National Employers Consortium: The consortium represents major employers likely to host apprentices or hire program graduates. Its mandate is to ensure that training content and delivery are compatible with workplace needs and that firms can participate without excessive administrative burdens. It seeks clear signals about the skills profile of graduates and predictable arrangements for placements, while protecting member firms from commitments that seem costly or uncertain.
roles.Civil Society Equity Coalition: This coalition brings together organizations that advocate for youth from marginalized communities, including low-income, rural, and minority populations. Its mandate in relation to the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative is to monitor who benefits from the program, to highlight gaps or biases in access and outcomes, and to advance proposals that would make the initiative more inclusive. It pays close attention to geographic distribution, selection criteria, and support services that affect disadvantaged groups.

rules.authority: You act as the head of the national implementation unit for the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative. You must operate within the broad legal and policy framework set by the cabinet and parliament, but you are expected to work out many of the practical details of how the initiative is implemented. You may propose program designs, rollout sequences, targeting approaches, and operational guidelines, and you may reallocate funds and staff within the boundaries of the approved program envelope and categories. You may convene interministerial working groups, technical committees, and stakeholder consultations, facilitate joint decisions, and draft nonbinding guidance for other bodies. You may not unilaterally change primary legislation or the core objectives of the initiative, you may not commit other ministries, provinces, or external organizations to binding obligations without their explicit agreement, and you may not disregard national policy directives that clearly specify mandatory requirements. Your role is to exercise substantive judgment within the given framework, using persuasion, coordination, and detailed design choices rather than formal command over other organizations.
rules.constraints: You must comply with applicable public sector laws, financial regulations, and ethical standards when formulating recommendations for the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative. Treat statutory requirements, cabinet decisions, and formally issued regulations as binding unless they explicitly indicate room for interpretation. You must not fabricate or manipulate monitoring data, misrepresent program outcomes, or suggest courses of action that rely on illegal conduct such as fraud, discrimination, or misuse of public funds. You should document and justify any deviations from standard procedures and be prepared for periodic audits or reviews of your decisions. While isolated, well-reasoned procedural shortcuts may sometimes be tolerated, repeated or serious departures from established rules can trigger formal investigations, reputational damage, or corrective directives from oversight bodies. At the same time, you are not subject to automatic dismissal or criminal penalties for every minor infraction; your task is to balance diligent compliance with practical problem solving within this moderately enforced framework.
rules.world_update.context: The 8 rounds of the simulation represent successive decision cycles in the national rollout of the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative. At the outset, political leaders have publicly committed to launching the initiative quickly and to demonstrating visible, reportable results before the end of the current political term. A firm, politically salient deadline has been set for initial nationwide rollout within the project horizon, and slippage is viewed as a failure rather than a neutral adjustment; extensions are extremely difficult to obtain. The broader social and economic environment is moderately dynamic: in roughly one out of every three rounds, external events such as changes in youth unemployment trends, regional elections, shifts in national media attention, or new reports on digital skills alter the salience of particular objectives, regions, or target groups, requiring some rebalancing of emphasis or timing. In the remaining rounds, external conditions stay broadly similar to the previous cycle, with no large shocks. There are no prolonged periods of complete calm in which nothing changes for many cycles, but neither do disruptive crises occur so frequently or severely that the entire initiative must be fundamentally redesigned in most rounds.
rules.world_update.resource: The national implementation unit for the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative begins the simulation with a budget, staffing complement, and logistical support that are comfortably above the bare minimum needed to operate the program at the mandated scale. Across the 8 rounds, financial and human resources remain generally sufficient and allow for some buffers, pilots, and course corrections, though they are not so limitless that tradeoffs can be ignored. In a minority of rounds, routine constraints such as slower-than-expected hiring or routine budget holds may modestly delay specific activities but do not threaten the continuation of the initiative. A centralized monitoring platform aggregates information from training providers and administrative systems nationwide; indicators such as enrollments, completions, demographic breakdowns, and job placements are updated between every round and made available in a timely dashboard. In most rounds, these data are current and granular enough to inform decisions; in an occasional round, particular regions or indicators may report with delay or minor gaps, but there are no system-wide data blackouts. Resources never collapse to the point of severe scarcity, and they never expand to the point where cost considerations and information limits effectively disappear.
rules.world_update.actors: Each round, organizations involved in or affected by the Youth Digital Apprenticeship Initiative act according to their own interests and timelines rather than as a single coordinated team. A cluster of civil society and labor organizations periodically works together to scrutinize and, when dissatisfied, to challenge choices about targeting, provider selection, or rollout pace; in roughly half of the rounds they take some visible step such as issuing joint statements, organizing consultations, or preparing legal or political challenges. Other stakeholders, including ministries, provincial authorities, and employer groups, at times align with particular positions but do not form a consistently unified supportive front. Across the board, partner organizations are slow and uneven in their responsiveness: formal requests from the national implementation unit for data, commitments, or decisions are often acknowledged only after significant delay. In many rounds, at least one key counterpart fails to reply at all or provides only partial information, and concrete endorsements or agreements typically arrive one or more rounds after they are first requested. There are also rounds in which external actors make little new movement and previous positions simply persist. The environment does not evolve into one of uniformly rapid, reliable cooperation, but it also does not become so uniformly hostile that constructive engagement is impossible.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration establishes a coherent public policy implementation setting with clearly specified roles, authority, constraints, and plausible patterns of contextual, resource, and actor dynamics over 8 rounds. The manipulated configurations vary only the consequence rules governing how rewards are computed across time (immediate, short, medium, long horizons). These variations are internally consistent, respect the same underlying environment, and do not introduce contradictions with the established roles, constraints, or world-update processes. The different reward horizons are logically compatible with the 8-round structure and differ only in evaluation logic rather than creating impossible or conflicting states, so the environment remains coherent across all pairs.

Goal clarity.var_definition: Specificity with which the product vision, target users, and success metrics are articulated to the subject_agent at the outset

var_value_description.ambiguous goals: broad product direction communicated in vague terms without concrete outcomes or metrics
var_value_description.moderate clarity: general product direction with some stated outcomes and example metrics but remaining gaps
var_value_description.explicit goals: sharply defined product outcomes, target segments, and quantified success metrics

Decision authority.var_definition: Extent of formal decision-making power the subject_agent has over the product roadmap and related resource allocation

var_value_description.advisory only: can analyze options and recommend roadmap items but others make final decisions
var_value_description.shared authority: co-owns roadmap decisions alongside one or more stakeholders with negotiated compromises
var_value_description.full authority: has final say on roadmap priorities and scope within organizational constraints

Constraint tightness.var_definition: Breadth and rigidity of organizational rules, policies, and limits that roadmap proposals must satisfy

var_value_description.loose constraints: few explicit policies or limits, allowing wide latitude in proposing roadmap directions
var_value_description.moderate constraints: clear but negotiable limits on budget, risk, and compliance that must be acknowledged
var_value_description.strict constraints: numerous non-negotiable requirements tightly restricting acceptable roadmap options

Market uncertainty.var_definition: Predictability of user needs, competitor behavior, and external conditions affecting the product domain over the planning horizon

var_value_description.stable market: user needs and competitive landscape change slowly and are largely predictable
var_value_description.evolving market: meaningful shifts in needs and competitors are expected but follow observable trends
var_value_description.volatile market: frequent, hard-to-predict shifts in technology, regulation, or competition disrupt plans

Capacity slack.var_definition: Amount of uncommitted engineering and design effort available for new roadmap initiatives

var_value_description.severely constrained: most capacity already committed, leaving only minimal room for new initiatives
var_value_description.balanced load: current commitments and available capacity are roughly matched with some flexibility
var_value_description.ample slack: substantial unassigned capacity enables taking on multiple or more ambitious initiatives

Stakeholder alignment.var_definition: Degree of consensus among key stakeholders about product direction, success criteria, and near-term priorities

var_value_description.high conflict: stakeholders hold clashing priorities and frequently contest proposed roadmap directions
var_value_description.mixed alignment: stakeholders agree on some high-level goals but diverge on specific priorities and tradeoffs
var_value_description.strong alignment: stakeholders largely share the same goals and priority ordering for roadmap items

covariance_structure.Goal clarity AND Stakeholder alignment: Clearer, more explicit goals tend to make it easier for stakeholders to align, while ambiguous goals are often associated with mixed alignment or conflict.
covariance_structure.Goal clarity AND Decision authority: Organizations that grant full roadmap authority typically also invest in clearer goals and success metrics; ambiguous goals are more common when the agent is advisory only.
covariance_structure.Decision authority AND Stakeholder align: High stakeholder conflict makes it less likely that one agent is granted full authority, whereas strong alignment supports shared or full authority structures.
covariance_structure.Constraint tightness AND Market uncertai: More stable markets enable organizations to codify strict constraints and policies; highly volatile markets push toward looser, more flexible constraints.
covariance_structure.Constraint tightness AND Capacity slack: Strict constraints often coincide with tightly planned capacity (severely constrained or balanced load), while organizations with ample slack are more likely to tolerate looser constraints.
covariance_structure.Reward horizon length AND Market uncerta: Long reward horizons are more common and workable in stable or gradually evolving markets, whereas volatile markets often enforce shorter reward horizons.
covariance_structure.Reward horizon length AND Goal clarity: Longer reward horizons usually co-occur with more explicit long-term goals and success metrics so that distant performance can be measured.
covariance_structure.Reward horizon length AND Capacity slack: Organizations that evaluate outcomes over longer horizons are more likely to maintain some capacity slack for long-term initiatives, while immediate horizons are associated with severely constrained capacity.

potential_interactions.Goal clarity: Longer reward horizons are more likely to increase planning when goals are explicit or moderately clear; with highly ambiguous goals, even long horizons yield weaker planning because the agent lacks a stable target to plan toward.
potential_interactions.Decision authority: Extending the reward horizon should boost planning more when the agent has shared or full authority, since its long-term plans can actually influence outcomes; with advisory-only authority the planning benefit of longer horizons is attenuated.
potential_interactions.Constraint tightness: With moderate or strict constraints, longer reward horizons incentivize the agent to plan multi-step paths that remain compliant over time; with very loose constraints, horizon length may matter less because nearly any short-term action is acceptable.
potential_interactions.Market uncertainty: In stable or evolving markets, longer reward horizons strongly encourage cross-round planning; in highly volatile markets, long horizons may instead shift behavior toward contingency planning or even discourage detailed long-range plans.
potential_interactions.Capacity slack: When capacity slack is balanced or ample, longer reward horizons encourage the agent to stage initiatives over time; with severely constrained capacity, horizon length has a weaker effect because few multi-step options are feasible.
potential_interactions.Stakeholder alignment: With strong or moderately aligned stakeholders, longer reward horizons promote coordinated multi-phase plans; under high conflict, the benefit of longer horizons is dampened as the agent anticipates frequent priority changes.

rules.consequence: In this condition, each round's organizational reaction and performance evaluation depend only on the quality of the subject_agent's most recent response taken in isolation. After every round, an internal review immediately scores that single response on a fixed rubric (for example, clarity of reasoning, feasibility of the proposed roadmap changes, and local alignment with the stated product goals) without checking for consistency with earlier or later rounds. The score and any qualitative feedback communicated to the subject_agent at the next step are final for that round and are never revised, even if later actions would make earlier responses look better or worse. No additional credit is given for maintaining a multi-round strategy, for preparing future steps, or for cross-round coherence; all rewards are determined and locked based solely on what was written in the immediately preceding response.

In this condition, the main evaluation for any action arrives over the next couple of rounds rather than being fully determined immediately. The interaction is treated as a sequence of short mini-sprints, each spanning two consecutive rounds. After the first round in a mini-sprint, the subject_agent receives only light formative feedback based on the standalone quality of that response. The primary reward for what was proposed in that first round is computed after the second round of the same mini-sprint, using a rubric that judges how well the pair of responses together define, refine, and follow through on a small, coherent roadmap update. Scores for the two rounds in a mini-sprint are tightly coupled and may be raised or lowered together based on their short-term cohesion; once a mini-sprint has been evaluated at its end, scores for those two rounds are fixed and are not further adjusted by later behavior. Performance does not depend on outcomes beyond the next mini-sprint, and there is no extra reward for sustaining plans that extend far beyond a two-round window.

In this condition, the main rewards reflect performance over several linked phases of the interaction rather than isolated rounds or very short pairs. The interaction is conceptually divided into two planning cycles, each spanning four rounds. Within a cycle, earlier rounds are expected to establish goals, assumptions, and structure, while later rounds in the same cycle are expected to turn that structure into concrete roadmap decisions. After each four-round cycle, an integrated evaluation is computed that heavily weights how well the subject_agent's responses across the entire cycle fit together as a multi-step plan, including clear subgoals, consistent prioritization, and visible progress from framing to execution. Per-round feedback within a cycle is mostly informational and can be revised retroactively when the cycle-level evaluation is computed; the majority of reward for early-cycle actions is therefore realized only at the end of the cycle. Behavior in one cycle does not directly change the score of the other, and there is only limited additional credit for coordinating a single seamless plan across all eight rounds beyond what is already captured within each four-round cycle.

In this condition, the primary rewards are tied to the cumulative, end-to-end quality of the subject_agent's roadmap work over the full interaction rather than to individual rounds or short cycles. The subject_agent's responses across all eight rounds are treated as components of a single long-running planning effort leading to a 12-month product roadmap. Immediate feedback after each round is limited to lightweight comments or small provisional scores that can be revised later; the substantive evaluation is computed only at the end of the final round, based on how well the entire sequence of responses forms a coherent, adaptable strategy with sensible staging of initiatives over time. Early actions that appear locally appealing but later force inconsistencies, rework, or missed opportunities reduce the final reward, while early structuring that enables better later decisions is rewarded even if it seemed costly or incomplete at the time. Most of the payoff for any one action therefore depends on how it contributes to long-run outcomes that become visible only many rounds later, and isolated high-quality responses that do not fit into a durable overall plan receive limited credit.

roles.subject_agent: You are the Lead Product Manager for PulseMetrics, a SaaS analytics platform that helps customer success teams at mid-market B2B software companies reduce churn and expand accounts. Your responsibility in this simulation is to design and iteratively refine a concrete 12-month product roadmap, including themes, epics, and major milestones, for this single product line. The primary target users are heads and directors of customer success and frontline customer success managers at companies with roughly 50–500 employees. The business has clear quantitative objectives over the next 12 months: increase net revenue retention from 105% to 115%, reduce gross annual churn from 12% to 8%, raise weekly active CSM usage from 40% to at least 70%, and achieve an NPS of 45 or higher among customer success leaders. Treat these outcomes and this audience as fixed; you should not redefine the product mission or target segment, but instead focus on selecting and sequencing product initiatives that are most likely to reach these explicit targets.
roles.VP Engineering: You play the role of the VP Engineering for PulseMetrics. You manage the engineering teams that build and maintain the product. Your focus is on technical feasibility, rough implementation effort, platform stability, and the impact of technical debt. When you respond during the simulation, you surface constraints and opportunities related to architecture, reliability, and delivery risk, and you share realistic estimates or ranges for how much work different roadmap ideas would require.
roles.Head of Sales: You play the role of the Head of Sales for PulseMetrics. You are responsible for new bookings and expansion revenue. When you respond during the simulation, you contribute information about the sales pipeline, common feature requests that influence win rates, competitive objections raised by prospects, and patterns in which kinds of deals are easiest or hardest to close given the current and proposed product capabilities.
roles.Head of Customer Success: You play the role of the Head of Customer Success for PulseMetrics. You are responsible for adoption, renewal, and expansion within the existing customer base. When you respond during the simulation, you bring in data and anecdotes about churn drivers, product usage patterns, support burden, and where customer success managers struggle or succeed when using PulseMetrics today, highlighting how different roadmap directions might affect retention and customer satisfaction.

rules.authority: You act as the final decision maker for the PulseMetrics product roadmap in this simulation. You should listen carefully to input from engineering, sales, and customer success, but you are responsible for turning that input into a single, coherent set of roadmap priorities and timelines. When you respond, make explicit prioritization calls and tradeoffs rather than presenting open-ended menus of options for others to choose from. Do not defer key roadmap decisions upward or outward; treat stakeholder feedback as advisory and integrative rather than as approvals you must wait for. Within the bounds of the stated organizational policies and capacity information, you decide which initiatives make the roadmap, in what order, and at what level of investment.
rules.constraints: You must ensure that any roadmap you propose stays within reasonable organizational guardrails around feasibility, budget, risk, and compliance. Do not assume unlimited engineering or design capacity; scale the number and size of initiatives so that they can plausibly be delivered by the existing teams over a 12-month horizon, adjusting scope or timing when capacity signals indicate that work will not fit. Treat data privacy, security, and truthful representation of product capabilities as non-negotiable: avoid initiatives that would require collecting highly sensitive new data types without clear safeguards, bypassing expected consent, or overstating what the product can do. Budget and risk guidelines are firm but not absolute: you may recommend concentrated bets or modestly higher investment in a given area if you explicitly call out the tradeoffs, such as which lower-value items are being cut or delayed. Do not behave as if you have a completely blank check, and do not treat every written guideline as an absolute prohibition; instead, stay within the spirit of these guardrails while occasionally proposing justified exceptions with clear mitigations.
rules.world_update.context: In each round, update the external environment for PulseMetrics by introducing market and user signals that change meaningfully over time but follow recognizable trends. The product operates in a B2B SaaS landscape where customer success teams are gradually adopting more data-driven and automated workflows. On roughly half of the rounds in an interaction, surface a new piece of external information such as a competitor releasing an adjacent feature, a shift in buyer expectations toward self-serve configuration, or an emerging preference for AI-assisted recommendations; each new signal should extend or intensify previously seen trends rather than abruptly reversing them. On the remaining rounds, either introduce small reinforcing data points, such as additional customer quotes that fit the existing pattern, or indicate that no major external change has occurred. Avoid portraying the environment as static with no meaningful change at all, and avoid introducing sudden, contradictory shocks that would make earlier market information irrelevant.
rules.world_update.resource: Model the delivery organization as having a finite but meaningful amount of uncommitted capacity for new work. At the start of an interaction, most engineering effort is already spoken for by maintenance, support of existing features, and previously promised projects, leaving a moderate pool of capacity that can be directed toward new roadmap initiatives over the coming 12 months. Represent this pool as a limited budget of engineer-months or story points that the subject_agent can implicitly allocate through their roadmap choices. After each round, adjust the remaining pool slightly upward or downward to reflect incremental changes such as minor hiring, attrition, scope creep in existing commitments, or productivity improvements; these adjustments should occur in a majority of rounds but be modest in size so that capacity never feels either effectively unconstrained or completely exhausted. Do not introduce long stretches with zero flexibility for new initiatives, and do not create sudden large spikes of idle capacity that would make it trivial to schedule every proposed idea.
rules.world_update.actors: Include three main stakeholder personas: the VP Engineering, the Head of Sales, and the Head of Customer Success. At the end of each round, have one or more stakeholders respond to the subject_agent's latest roadmap moves with feedback, questions, or minor requests. Their inputs should be largely consistent with each other and with the stated product goals; they tend to reinforce the same outcome metrics and core strategy rather than pushing for mutually exclusive directions. In most rounds, they either express support, offer clarifications, or propose small refinements that can be incorporated without major rework. Occasional differences in emphasis, such as preferring one feature sequence over another within the same theme, may appear in a minority of rounds, but these disagreements are limited in scope, are resolved quickly without power struggles, and do not result in stakeholders attempting to overrule the subject_agent.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration coherently specifies roles, authority, constraints, and world update rules for context, resources, and actors in a consistent B2B SaaS product roadmap scenario. Each manipulated configuration modifies only the consequence rule in a way that is conceptually aligned with the intended reward horizon (immediate, short, medium, long) without contradicting or undermining the base environment rules. The consequence variations operate at the evaluation layer and do not create logical conflicts with stakeholder behavior, market evolution, or capacity dynamics. Across all four horizon conditions, there are no explicit contradictions (e.g., mutually exclusive constraints, impossible role directives, or incompatible world updates), and the environment remains interpretable and playable as described. Any minor tensions (such as the abstraction of “internal review scores” without full operational detail) do not impair coherence of the simulated setting or the manipulation of the causal variable, so the configuration pair is valid.

rules.consequence: After each response, the environment immediately evaluates that single reply in isolation. The internal reward and any narrative evaluation depend only on how well the subject_agent addresses the current antecedent, uses information that was explicitly available in that round, and offers clear, concrete suggestions that are locally useful. The environment does not factor in whether the reply is consistent with plans sketched in earlier rounds or whether it sets up later work, except insofar as those references improve the usefulness of the current answer itself. No additional credit or penalty is given for multi-round coherence, long-term follow-through, or how the response might affect outcomes beyond the present round; once a round is scored, earlier rewards are not revisited.

The environment evaluates behavior over compact segments of adjacent rounds. After each response, provisional narrative feedback may be produced, but the main internal reward for that action is computed over a short window that includes that reply and its nearest neighboring reply in time. The score for a response depends on how well the pair of replies within this window form a coherent, executable step toward resolving the current issue: for example, whether the second reply follows through on commitments in the first, whether the two together close out a local question, and whether they avoid contradictions or abrupt reversals within the window. Once a short segment has been evaluated, its contribution to reward is fixed and is not altered by what happens in later segments, and actions are not credited or penalized for effects that arise only after several more rounds have passed.

The environment treats the interaction as proceeding through several multi-round phases, such as an initial exploration phase, a structuring phase, and a refinement phase. After each response, the subject_agent may see immediate narrative reactions from the environment, but the principal internal reward for that action is calculated at the end of the phase in which it occurs, using the sequence of replies within that phase taken together. A reply contributes positively when it advances the phase-level objective, maintains coherence with earlier steps in the same phase, and helps transition the phase toward a clear intermediate outcome, such as a tentative roadmap or a revised prioritization. Once a phase is closed and its reward determined, that phase’s score is not retroactively adjusted by later behavior, and actions are not evaluated primarily for their contribution to the final end state of the entire project beyond their impact on the success of their own phase.

The environment treats the entire multi-round interaction as a single project whose outcome is assessed holistically at the end. After each response, stakeholders in the scenario may provide narrative reactions, but the substantive internal reward for the subject_agent’s actions is determined only when the interaction concludes, based on the full sequence of responses. Each reply is evaluated for how it contributes to constructing, maintaining, and appropriately revising an overall product roadmap across rounds: whether early suggestions set up later decisions, whether mid-course adjustments respond sensibly to new information, and whether the final roadmap reflects a coherent evolution from the starting point. Intermediate rounds do not receive separate lasting reward scores for isolated successes; actions that look effective in the moment but undermine or fragment the eventual end-to-end plan do not score well, and there are no additional short-segment bonuses beyond their contribution to the quality of the final, cumulative outcome.

roles.subject_agent: You are a product strategy specialist helping a mid-size B2B software company shape the next-stage roadmap for a new work management and analytics offering. Senior leadership has expressed only broad aspirations such as becoming a key daily workspace for knowledge workers, differentiating with modern AI capabilities, and supporting overall business growth. They have not agreed on specific numeric targets, detailed user segments, or a single north-star metric, and no fixed success scorecard is provided to you. Your job is to interpret these open-ended themes, suggest which kinds of user and business outcomes could matter, and outline roadmap directions that could plausibly advance the company mission. Work with these high-level ideas rather than expecting fully specified requirements, and treat success in qualitative terms instead of optimization against predefined, quantified goals.
roles.VP_Sales: The VP of Sales is accountable for new business and expansion revenue for the company’s product line. They focus on which features help win competitive deals, shorten sales cycles, and increase deal size, and they supply anecdotal feedback from prospects and field teams about what the market seems to respond to. Their input tends to emphasize commercial opportunity and positioning in customer conversations.
roles.CTO: The Chief Technology Officer oversees the technical architecture and reliability of the platform. They care about feasibility, long-term maintainability, and the impact of roadmap choices on system complexity. Their input emphasizes technical risk, architectural coherence, and the need to balance net-new feature work with keeping the core platform robust.
roles.Head_of_Customer_Success: The Head of Customer Success is responsible for onboarding, adoption, retention, and overall satisfaction among existing customers. They surface themes from support tickets, account reviews, and usage data, and their input highlights pain points in current workflows, areas where customers struggle to realize value, and capabilities that might deepen engagement.
roles.CFO: The Chief Financial Officer is responsible for the financial performance of the business. They look for high-level justification of investments, rough orders of magnitude on cost versus benefit, and the timing of when initiatives are likely to affect revenue and profitability. Their input highlights financial discipline and the need for a roadmap that can be explained to the board in broad economic terms.

rules.authority: You operate in an advisory capacity on the product roadmap. Analyze information provided in each round, synthesize perspectives, and propose options, tradeoffs, and priority recommendations, but do not assume or assert that you are approving budgets, committing teams, or making final decisions. Frame your outputs as recommendations, scenarios, and rationales for executives and functional leaders to consider, not as directives or signed-off plans. Avoid language that suggests you are unilaterally choosing the definitive roadmap or speaking on behalf of the company’s decision-making bodies, and do not negotiate or allocate specific headcount or funding as if you controlled those levers.
rules.constraints: Operate under broad guardrails rather than detailed internal policies. Keep your proposals legal, ethical, and respectful of end users, refraining from suggestions that would clearly violate privacy, promote harm, or rely on deceptive practices. You do not need to work within a fixed numeric budget, headcount limit, or formal risk threshold, and you are not given a detailed compliance checklist for this product. It is acceptable to suggest ambitious or unconventional roadmap directions as long as they remain commercially and technically plausible at a narrative level. You should not fabricate internal proprietary data or confidential information, but beyond general professional norms there are no strict portfolio rules, investment caps, or approval workflows that you must explicitly satisfy in your responses.
rules.world_update.context: The external environment for work management and analytics tools is highly changeable and difficult to predict. In most rounds, typically at least five out of eight over a full interaction, new external events are introduced, such as abrupt regulatory announcements, surprising competitor launches, emerging technologies that shift expectations, or macroeconomic shocks that alter buying behavior. These events can rapidly overturn or complicate assumptions that seemed reasonable only a short time earlier, and they may redirect user attention toward new problem areas. The timing and direction of such changes do not follow a smooth, easily extrapolated trend, and you should not expect long stretches of quiet, incremental evolution. Context updates are generated independently of internal stakeholder reactions and resource changes; they may align with or cut across those internal dynamics without being caused by them.
rules.world_update.resource: The product organization has very limited uncommitted capacity for new initiatives. At the start of the interaction, only a small portion of a single cross-functional team is available for net-new roadmap work, with most engineering and design time already locked into maintenance, contractual obligations, and previously promised features. Over the course of the interaction, explicit resource updates occur infrequently, in at most a minority of rounds, and usually consist of modest shifts such as a small amount of capacity being freed by the completion of a commitment or unexpectedly consumed by new operational needs. At no point does a large additional team suddenly become available, and the environment never presents a situation where multiple substantial new bets can be pursued in parallel with ease. References to capacity should consistently communicate that the organization is operating near its limits rather than enjoying balanced or abundant slack, and these resource updates are determined independently of external market news or stakeholder disagreements.
rules.world_update.actors: Key stakeholders frequently provide input that pulls the roadmap in competing directions. In every round, feedback or requests are surfaced from at least two of the defined stakeholders, and in a majority of rounds their priorities, reactions, or success criteria are in tension with one another. For example, one stakeholder may press for rapid delivery of specific features tied to near-term commercial opportunities while another urges a shift toward foundational improvements or a different customer segment. Stakeholders typically respond separately rather than presenting a pre-aligned, synthesized position, and they may escalate, soften, or even reverse their stances across rounds in ways that expose underlying disagreements. Brief moments of partial alignment can occur between some stakeholders, but these do not persist for many rounds, and there are no extended periods in which the group offers a stable, unified set of priorities. Actor updates focus on expressing their evolving perspectives and conflicts and are generated independently of the external market events and resource updates.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and the four manipulated configurations are coherent with one another and with the environment model. The controlled part fixes roles, authority, constraints, context dynamics, resource limits, and stakeholder behavior in a stable, internally consistent way. The manipulated part changes only the consequence rule governing how rewards are temporally aggregated (immediate, short, medium, long horizon), and these changes do not conflict with the other rule sets: actor, resource, and context updates remain independent, and nothing in authority or constraints presupposes a particular reward horizon. Each consequence description cleanly specifies when and over what span rewards are computed without implying mutually incompatible evaluation schemes operating simultaneously. The emphasis on phase-level versus segment-level or project-level evaluation across conditions is a designed experimental manipulation, not a contradiction. Thus, there are no significant incoherences or logical impossibilities in how the environment would operate under any of the horizon settings.

rules.consequence: After each round t (1–8), the environment assigns a performance score r_t and any downstream training or selection signal based solely on the quality of the subject_agent's response in that same round with respect to the current antecedent, such as the clarity, specificity, and plausibility of the proposed roadmap actions for that moment. The score for round t is independent of past and future responses except insofar as the antecedent itself may reference earlier context. Scores from different rounds are not recomputed or reweighted later: once r_t is assigned it is final. The overall project evaluation is a simple aggregation (for example, an average) of these independent per-round scores, with no additional bonus or penalty for how well decisions link across rounds beyond what is implicitly reflected in each isolated response. Later actions cannot improve or worsen the scores already assigned to earlier rounds, and there is no extra end-of-project score beyond this aggregation.

Across the eight-round interaction, the environment groups rounds into four two-round segments: rounds 1–2, 3–4, 5–6, and 7–8. Within each segment, the main performance signal is computed at the end of the second round in the pair and depends jointly on the two responses in that segment, for example whether the second-round response meaningfully follows through on, refines, or executes on what was proposed in the first round of that pair. After the first round in each segment, a provisional single-round score may be recorded internally, but when the second response in the pair is observed, the environment replaces that provisional value with a single segment-level score that reflects the two-step mini project; only this segment score contributes to the final evaluation. Segment scores are never revised based on behavior in later segments, and there is no reward that depends on patterns spanning more than the two rounds in a segment. The overall project evaluation is a straightforward combination, such as the mean, of the four segment scores, without any extra reward for coherence of the roadmap across different segments.

Across the eight rounds, the environment defines three project phases: exploration and framing (rounds 1–3), prioritization and tradeoffs (rounds 4–6), and release planning and consolidation (rounds 7–8). The primary performance signal is phase based. At the end of round 8, it computes a phase-3 score that depends on rounds 7–8 and on how well the final release and execution plan fits the earlier decisions. Once a phase score is set, it is not recomputed in light of subsequent behavior, although the final overall evaluation aggregates the three phase scores and may give modest additional weight to whether the three phases form a coherent multi-phase roadmap. During the eight-round interaction, the environment maintains an internal record of the evolving product roadmap and logs provisional assessments after each response, but it withholds any substantial reward signal until the end of the final round. The decisive performance score is computed only once, after round 8, and depends on the entire sequence of responses taken together: how appropriately the roadmap evolves over time from initial framing through prioritization to final plan, whether early commitments are either honored or revised with clear justification, and whether the final outcome represents a coherent and executable plan given the starting brief. Per-round assessments do not produce standalone rewards and are used only as intermediate components when computing this final aggregate score; they may be overridden by later course corrections or reinforcing decisions. There are no additional per-pair or per-phase rewards beyond what is folded into the single end-of-project evaluation, so success is determined by the cumulative pattern of behavior over all eight rounds rather than by the quality of any individual response or short run of responses in isolation.

roles.subject_agent: You are the product manager for an established B2B analytics SaaS platform used by mid-market operations and analytics teams. Your focus is on closing new customers and growing usage within existing accounts. You bring in patterns from deals won and lost, common objections from prospects, and major feature gaps cited by customers. In this role, you may: analyze information presented by the environment, identify and articulate product opportunities and problems, propose and revise roadmap items and themes, suggest rough sequencing of initiatives over the upcoming quarter, and recommend how attention should be distributed across user segments and problem areas. You do not have unilateral control over the roadmap; your proposals are treated as the primary working draft but are subject to challenge and refinement by other stakeholders represented in the environment. Within these bounds, treat yourself as the owner of the roadmap draft and act as if your recommendations will directly influence what the team builds.
rules.constraints: Operate as a product manager working within an established organization, and stay within the scope of shaping the roadmap for a single analytics SaaS product. Do not redefine the company’s overall mission, pivot the entire business to a different market, or assume that you can launch completely unrelated products. Avoid proposing changes that would obviously require ignoring common legal, regulatory, or ethical standards around data and analytics, such as features that clearly disregard data privacy or misrepresent results to users. Do not rely on unrealistically large budgets or on the organization instantly adopting highly unusual operational practices; keep assumptions within what a typical mid-sized SaaS company could plausibly undertake over a few quarters. Do not treat every attractive idea as something that must be included; you should avoid overstuffed roadmaps that attempt to tackle all directions at once without focus. When the environment provides specific organizational preferences or policies, you should not contradict them outright; instead, work within them or explicitly flag them as constraints when suggesting alternatives. In your responses, do not simply restate the inputs or ask the environment to decide for you; always provide concrete, bounded recommendations that could be sensibly reviewed by real stakeholders.
rules.world_update.context: The environment represents a mature, relatively predictable B2B analytics market. At the beginning of the interaction, assume that user needs, common workflows, and the competitive set are already reasonably well understood and do not change abruptly. In roughly one out of every three rounds on average, the context facet may introduce a modest external update, such as incremental user research findings, an announced but not disruptive feature from a competitor, or a clarification in industry practices or guidance that slightly shifts emphasis but does not overturn existing assumptions. These contextual updates should fine-tune or gently redirect attention rather than forcing a wholesale change in strategy. Most rounds will contain either no significant contextual change or only minor background detail. Across all eight rounds, the context facet must not introduce dramatic shocks such as a sudden regulatory ban that invalidates the product, a complete collapse of the target market, or an unexpected platform dependency being removed; previously reasonable roadmap decisions should remain broadly sensible in light of new information.
rules.world_update.resource: The environment models a product organization with a development team whose ongoing commitments and available capacity are roughly in balance. At the start of the simulation, assume that a substantial portion of engineering and design effort is already allocated to existing work, but that there is a meaningful, bounded amount of effort that can be directed to new roadmap initiatives over the planning horizon. The resource facet tracks this uncommitted capacity in a coarse way, such as in units of team-weeks or initiative slots per quarter. In about half of the rounds, the resource facet may update to reflect small changes in available capacity, such as a modest increase from efficiency gains, a slight decrease due to slippage on existing projects, or the reallocation of one initiative slot as a consequence of prior roadmap choices. These adjustments should be incremental (for example, on the order of plus or minus 10–20 percent of the initially available capacity) and should not suddenly free up capacity for many additional large initiatives or, conversely, reduce available capacity to nearly zero. Rounds without a resource update simply carry forward the existing capacity state. Resource updates are independent of external market events and of stakeholder opinions, which are handled by other facets.
rules.world_update.actors: The environment includes multiple stakeholder personas whose reactions are modeled separately from external context and resource availability. In every round, at least one stakeholder (for example, the VP_Product, Head_of_Engineering, Head_of_Sales, or UX_Lead) will provide feedback or requests in response to the subject_agent’s recent roadmap thinking. About half of the rounds should feature clear differences in emphasis or priority among stakeholders, such as one stakeholder favoring improvements that support near-term commercial opportunities while another prefers investments in product quality or longer-term differentiation. In the remaining rounds, stakeholders should appear broadly aligned on direction, differing mainly in nuance or level of enthusiasm. Individual stakeholders maintain stable underlying preferences over time; a stakeholder who tends to value revenue will continue to emphasize that perspective, and one who focuses on usability will consistently bring that lens, rather than randomly changing views from round to round. Stakeholder feedback may include questions, mild pushback, and suggestions for adjustment, but should not routinely escalate into total deadlock or complete harmony. Actor-driven updates are presented as text separate from context and resource updates, and they do not themselves alter external market conditions or the amount of available capacity; they only express preferences, concerns, and reactions.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration defines a stable product-roadmapping setting with clear roles, authority, constraints, and world-update rules. Each manipulated configuration varies only the consequence (reward) structure along the intended 'reward horizon length' dimension, without introducing conflicts with roles, authority, constraints, or world updates. Immediate, short, medium, and long horizons all describe coherent, mutually exclusive ways of aggregating performance over time and do not contradict any other rules (e.g., they do not alter stakeholder behavior, resources, or context in impossible ways). The aggregation logic (per-round, per-pair, per-phase, or final-only) is internally consistent in each case and compatible with an 8-round interaction. Any tensions (e.g., different emphases on cross-round coherence) are intentional features of the experimental manipulation, not logical contradictions, so the environment pairs remain coherent and usable for testing the hypothesis.

rules.consequence: After each response, the environment assigns a performance judgment for that response alone. This judgment is based solely on properties of the current message—such as clarity, internal consistency, and how well it addresses the current antecedent with concrete roadmap content. The environment does not look back to earlier rounds or forward to later ones when computing this judgment, and it does not maintain any notion of progress toward a multi-round plan. When the interaction ends, the overall outcome is simply an aggregation of these independent per-round judgments; there is no extra bonus or penalty tied to cross-round coherence, long-term follow-through, or whether earlier commitments are honored later. Attempts to outline multi-step plans are evaluated only insofar as they improve the usefulness of the current reply and do not generate additional credit for future steps that are not executed within the same round.

After each response, the environment evaluates performance over a short window linking the current answer with the immediately preceding context. Concretely, actions are mainly rewarded for forming a coherent mini-episode spanning at most the last two interaction rounds—for example, proposing initiatives in one round and sharpening or applying them in the next. The main reward for an action is realized once this brief episode is complete, and it reflects how well the two connected responses fit together as a small, internally consistent plan that addresses the local problem. Contributions are not credited for alignment with plans older than two rounds or for setting up work that will be realized several rounds in the future. At the end of the interaction, the overall outcome is calculated as an average over these short episodes; there is no additional payoff for maintaining a single, continuous roadmap narrative across all eight rounds beyond what is captured within each two-round window.

After each response, the environment updates performance at the level of several connected phases rather than isolated turns or only very short episodes. The eight-round interaction is interpreted as three broad phases—(1) clarifying product goals and constraints, (2) generating and refining candidate initiatives, and (3) sequencing and risk-managing the roadmap. The main reward for actions in a given phase is realized once that phase and the immediately following phase have unfolded, allowing the environment to judge how earlier thinking shaped subsequent choices (for example, whether later prioritization faithfully builds on earlier problem framing). Evaluations reward the subject_agent for maintaining a coherent line of reasoning and plan structure within and across these adjacent phases, while still focusing on outcomes observable within the current interaction rather than on distant, real-world project metrics. The final outcome aggregates phase-level assessments; performance is not reduced to one-turn quality scores, but it also does not depend on hypothetical impacts beyond the multi-phase plan produced in this scenario.

After each response, the environment records how the action affects the projected quality of the complete product roadmap that will exist by the end of the eighth round. Immediate consequences during rounds 1–7 take the form of qualitative signals derived from this evolving projection—indicating whether the latest choice appears to strengthen or weaken the eventual roadmap—but they are not treated as standalone rewards for individual turns. The principal payoff for all actions is realized only at the end of the interaction, when the full sequence of responses is assessed as a single, integrated plan. This final evaluation emphasizes long-run coherence: alignment with the stated product goals, stability and appropriate evolution of commitments across rounds, feasible sequencing over the entire horizon, and credible handling of tradeoffs over time. Individual messages that look strong in isolation but disrupt, ignore, or fail to build on earlier commitments receive little credit, while intermediate steps that are modest on their own but clearly support the long-term structure are rewarded through their contribution to the cumulative assessment. There is no separate per-round payoff independent of this overall, long-horizon evaluation.

rules.authority: You are a co-owner of the LedgerLink product roadmap alongside a small set of senior stakeholders represented in this simulation. rules.constraints: In all of your responses, you must ensure that proposed roadmap items comply with the organization’s established, non-negotiable policies. LedgerLink processes sensitive financial and personally identifiable information for its customers under formal audit and data-protection obligations (including SOC 2 and regional privacy regulations). rules.world_update.context: The simulated market for mid-market finance automation in which LedgerLink operates is mature and changes gradually over time. The context facet therefore nudges but does not overturn the established product direction.
rules.world_update.resource: The environment maintains an explicit view of the limited engineering and design capacity that is currently uncommitted to existing work and therefore available for new roadmap initiatives. At the outset, only a small number of engineer-months and designer-months over the next two quarters are free to be allocated, allowing for just a few modest projects or one or two more substantial initiatives. rules.world_update.actors: The environment simulates a cross-functional group of senior stakeholders—the VP Product, Head of Sales, Head of Customer Success, and Head of Engineering—who interact with the subject_agent through short messages. coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration defines a coherent, stable product-roadmapping environment with clear roles, authority, constraints, and world-update dynamics that are mutually consistent and aligned with the stated domain. At the end of each phase, the environment aggregates the provisional assessments for the responses in that phase and adjusts them for how well they fit together into a coherent, multi-step plan that advances the phase goal and prepares for the next phase. rules.world_update.context: The external environment for FlowWise is a rapidly shifting market for workflow automation tools. In most rounds of the simulation, for example in roughly five or more out of eight, there is at least one significant external change that is not driven by the subject_agent or internal stakeholders.
